Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.

Studio | Quickstart | Showcase | Playground | Catalog | Docs | Discord

Download the desktop app: macOS · Windows · Linux (.deb)

HyperFrames is a free, open-source framework for turning HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into deterministic MP4 videos. Use it locally with the CLI, from AI coding agents with skills, or as the rendering core behind hosted authoring workflows.

The HyperFrames Studio app is free to use as well; its Pro plan adds HeyGen's top video, image, voice and music models.

Using Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or another coding agent? Run npx hyperframes skills update once, then ask your agent to make a video.

Quick Start

With an AI coding agent

For Claude Code, install the versioned plugin:

claude plugin marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes
claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes

To enable auto-update for the hyperframes marketplace, run claude in a terminal in your project. In Claude Code's terminal UI, run /plugin, then select Marketplaces → hyperframes → Enable auto-update. Afterward, use /hyperframes:hyperframes. See the plugin guide for Copilot, VS Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, updates, and migration.

For standalone skills (including OpenCode), use:

npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The picker opens with nothing pre-selected — the Core Skills group is all you need; /slideshow, /remotion-to-hyperframes and /figma install on demand. Without the picker (a script or a CI job), npx hyperframes skills update installs exactly the core set, whereas skills add --all installs all 9 published skills. The six repo-internal skills under .claude/skills / .agents/skills are excluded by default. For the full published set use npx hyperframes skills.

skills add resolves the skills.sh registry blob, which can lag main by hours. npx hyperframes skills update installs the skills from the release tag that matches your CLI version, so they match the CLI that runs them.

Run project-local installs from your video project's directory. From a HyperFrames checkout, use npx hyperframes skills update for a global install instead: a project-local installer target can overlap the tracked skills/ source and overwrite uncommitted edits. See contributor setup.

Try a prompt like:

Using /hyperframes, create a 10-second product intro with a fade-in title, a background video, and subtle background music.

The skills teach agents the HyperFrames production loop: plan the video, write valid HTML, wire seekable animations, add media, lint, preview, and render. They work with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, IBM Bob, and other coding agents that support skills.

Skills

HyperFrames ships 9 skills. Make any video by asking for it; the /hyperframes skill carries the contract and the references (film, captions, overlays, motion, look). Read it first.

For standalone installation, default to the core set (/hyperframes, /hyperframes-cli, /hyperframes-registry, /media-use, /reverse-any-video, /style-sampling). npx hyperframes skills update installs exactly that from anywhere; the interactive picker (npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes) lists it as the "Core Skills" group, nothing pre-selected. The picker is interactive-only — a non-interactive or agent run without --skill installs all 9. Use npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --all to install the complete published set deliberately (skips the picker), or npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --skill <name> for just one (bare name, no leading /).

Standalone installs stay lean after that: npx hyperframes init installs the core set only when it is missing and never touches a skill you already have (npx hyperframes skills update refreshes them, and never removes one); /figma, /slideshow and /remotion-to-hyperframes install on demand with npx hyperframes skills update <name>. Nothing re-pulls the full set behind your back.

Plugin packages

Plugins bundle the full skill catalog and use their agent's update manager. bun run package:agent-plugin builds the committed portable ZIP, source metadata, and SHA-256 checksum. See the maintainer checklist.

Upload to Codex

Build the upload-ready Codex plugin archive from the committed HEAD version of the manifest, brand assets, and skills:

bun run package:codex-plugin

This writes dist/hyperframes-plugin.zip with a hyperframes/ root folder and fails if the archive exceeds Codex's 100 MB upload limit.

Core set

Skill Use when
/hyperframes Read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays with HyperFrames (HTML rendered to video). Holds the render contract and the work loop, and points to the references for format, motion, look, captions, whole films and storyboards.
/hyperframes-cli The HyperFrames CLI by job — scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render locally or in the cloud, share, project history — plus reading its JSON and recovering from build or render failures.
/hyperframes-registry About 450 ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source — transitions, overlays, titles, kinetic type, captions, charts, maps, 3D, camera moves. Use before hand-building any named visual; also for hyperframes add and catalog.
/media-use Get or make any media for a video — music, sound effects, images, icons, logos, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades and looks — with HeyGen or free local tools, and mix placed audio. Also for footage that looks dark, flat or dull.
/reverse-any-video Rebuilding any video file as an editable HyperFrames project (motion graphics, talking heads, live action, AI-generated footage), checked frame by frame against the original. HyperFrames Pro.
/style-sampling Making a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles: Collage Explainer, Finance Explainer, Animated Science Explainer, 3D Brand Explainer, 3D True Crime. HyperFrames Pro.

On demand

Skill Use when
/figma Bring Figma into a video — rendered assets, brand tokens, components, storyboard frames as reconstructed motion, shaders and connector-assisted motion. Use when you paste a figma.com link.
/slideshow A presentation, pitch deck or interactive deck — discrete slides, fragment reveals, branching, hotspot navigation, presenter mode with speaker notes. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
/remotion-to-hyperframes Bringing existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, other tools' renders), verified frame by frame.

For visual design handoff workflows, see the Claude Design guide and Open Design guide.

Manually with the CLI

npx hyperframes init my-video
cd my-video
npx hyperframes preview      # preview in browser with live reload
npx hyperframes render       # render to MP4

Requirements: Node.js 22+, FFmpeg

What You Can Build

Need ideas? Browse the Showcase for finished videos you can watch, read, run, and remix.

  • Product launch videos and feature announcements
  • PR walkthroughs with animated code diffs, narration, and captions
  • Data visualizations, chart races, and map animations
  • Social videos with kinetic captions, overlays, and music
  • Docs-to-video, PDF-to-video, and site-tour explainers
  • Reusable motion graphics for automated content pipelines

Frame.md

frame.md — your design system, ready for video.

Every brand has a design.md. None of them were written for a camera. frame.md is the missing translation layer: it takes your web-context design spec and inverts it for the frame — the same tokens, the same rules, but rewritten so an AI agent can compose a promo video without guessing at scale or reaching for web chrome.

The output is a DESIGN.md superset your whole toolchain can read. Atoms stay sacred. Composition stays free. Numbers come from the script.


Biennale Yellow
BlockFrame

Blue Professional
Bold Poster

Broadside
Capsule

Cartesian
Cobalt Grid

Coral
Creative Mode

Browse and remix them all at hyperframes.studio/design.

How It Works

Define a video as HTML. Add data attributes for timing and tracks. Use GSAP, CSS, Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, WAAPI, or your own frame adapter for seekable animation.

<div id="stage" data-composition-id="launch" data-start="0" data-width="1920" data-height="1080">
  <video
    class="clip"
    data-start="0"
    data-duration="6"
    data-track-index="0"
    src="intro.mp4"
    muted
    playsinline
  ></video>

  <h1 id="title" class="clip" data-start="1" data-duration="4" data-track-index="1">Launch day</h1>

  <audio
    data-start="0"
    data-duration="6"
    data-track-index="2"
    data-volume="0.5"
    src="music.wav"
  ></audio>

  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/gsap@3/dist/gsap.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
    tl.from("#title", { opacity: 0, y: 40, duration: 0.8 }, 1);
    window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
    window.__timelines.launch = tl;
  </script>
</div>

Preview instantly in the browser. Render locally or in Docker. The renderer seeks each frame in headless Chrome and encodes the result with FFmpeg, so the same input produces the same video.

HyperFrames Stack

HyperFrames is the open-source rendering engine, plus a growing set of tools around HTML-native video creation.

Piece Status What it does
CLI Available Scaffold, preview, lint, inspect, and render local video projects
Core / Engine / Producer Available Parse compositions, drive headless Chrome, encode video, and mix audio
Catalog Available Reusable blocks and components for transitions, overlays, captions, charts, maps, and effects
Agent skills Available Teach coding agents the video-production patterns that generic web docs miss
Studio Available, evolving Browser surface for previewing and editing compositions
AWS Lambda rendering Available Deploy a distributed render stack and drive renders from your laptop or CI
hyperframes.studio Available Community playground for previewing, iterating, sharing, and rendering HTML-native video projects
frame.md Available Invert your design system for the camera — a DESIGN.md superset an agent can compose video from

Catalog

Install ready-to-use blocks and components:

npx hyperframes add flash-through-white   # shader transition
npx hyperframes add instagram-follow      # social overlay
npx hyperframes add data-chart            # animated chart

Browse the catalog at hyperframes.heygen.com/catalog.

Why HyperFrames?

  • HTML-native: compositions are HTML files with data attributes. No React requirement, no proprietary timeline format.
  • Agent-friendly: agents already write HTML, and the CLI is non-interactive by default.
  • Deterministic: same input, same frames, same output. Built for CI, regression tests, and automated rendering.
  • No build step: an index.html composition plays as-is and can be previewed directly in the browser.
  • Adapter-based animation: bring GSAP, CSS animations, Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, WAAPI, or a custom runtime.
  • Open source: Apache 2.0 license, with no per-render fees or commercial-use thresholds.

HyperFrames vs Remotion

HyperFrames is inspired by Remotion. Both tools render video with headless Chrome and FFmpeg. The main difference is the authoring model: Remotion's bet is React components; HyperFrames' bet is plain HTML that humans and agents can both write easily.

HyperFrames Remotion
Authoring HTML + CSS + seekable animation React components
Build step None; index.html plays as-is Bundler required
Agent handoff Plain HTML files JSX / React project
Library-clock animations Seekable, frame-accurate via adapters Wall-clock animation patterns need care
Distributed rendering Local and AWS Lambda render paths Remotion Lambda, mature cloud renderer
License Apache 2.0 Source-available Remotion License

Read the full comparison in the HyperFrames vs Remotion guide.

Documentation

Full documentation: hyperframes.heygen.com/introduction

  • Quickstart
  • Showcase
  • Guides
  • API Reference
  • Catalog
  • Examples
  • AWS Lambda rendering

Packages

Package Description
hyperframes CLI for creating, previewing, linting, and rendering compositions
@hyperframes/core Types, parsers, generators, linter, runtime, and frame adapters
@hyperframes/engine Seekable page-to-video capture engine using Puppeteer and FFmpeg
@hyperframes/producer Full rendering pipeline for capture, encode, and audio mix
@hyperframes/studio Browser-based composition editor UI
@hyperframes/player Embeddable <hyperframes-player> web component
@hyperframes/shader-transitions WebGL shader transitions for compositions
@hyperframes/aws-lambda AWS Lambda SDK and deployment surface for distributed renders

Community

HyperFrames is used in production at HeyGen, with community examples from teams like tldraw, TanStack, and others in ADOPTERS.md. Open a PR if your team is using HyperFrames.

  • Questions and ideas: Discord
  • Bugs and feature requests: GitHub Issues
  • User research: Book a casual 30-minute conversation with the HyperFrames team — no preparation or sales pitch
  • Security reports: SECURITY.md
  • Contributions: CONTRIBUTING.md

Development Note

The repo uses Git LFS for golden regression-test baselines under packages/producer/tests/**/output.mp4 (about 240 MB of .mp4 files). If you're cloning the full repo for development, install Git LFS first:

# macOS
brew install git-lfs

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install git-lfs

# Windows
winget install GitHub.GitLFS

# Then, once per machine
git lfs install

If you only need source files, you can skip LFS content:

GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1 git clone https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes.git

License

Apache 2.0

Share a video for review

Sign in with npx hyperframes auth login, then run npx hyperframes share to choose who can open the rendered review. Use share --update when edits should become a new version and share --manage for web settings. CLI and Desktop use the same sharing system and five free projects per workspace. Existing legacy published links remain reachable.

item.title: Vincentwei1021/video-shotcraft
item.description:
AI video skill for Claude Code & Codex — cinematic, editable product promos with Remotion: 124 shot recipe cards, 150 motion previews, beat sync, sound design, Motion Workbench & JianYing (CapCut CN) export.

https://vincentwei1021.github.io/video-shotcraft/

video-shotcraft

English | 中文 | 繁體中文 | 日本語 | Русский

▶ Browse all 150 shots in the Gallery · 🎬 Watch the Showcase

What it does

Tell Claude Code or Codex "make a promo for my product". The agent captures your real pages, picks shots from a library of tuned motion recipes, storyboards the film, animates it with Remotion, cuts it to the beat, adds sound design, checks every frame and hands you a finished MP4 you can keep editing.

It is not a video generator. Every frame is drawn by code from your own screenshots and copy, so the result is sharp, on-brand and fully editable.

How it works

What's new

Important

🎬 2026-10 · Shot library refresh

All 216 demos were polished and reviewed. The best versions now make up 124 cards / 150 shots, with fresh Gallery previews and video-shotcraft branding.

  • 2026-09 · Motion Workbench. Keep editing the delivered film in a CapCut-style browser editor.
  • 2026-08 · video-talkcraft, the narration-video sibling: script + voiceover in, every motion beat locked to the voice (78 narration previews).
  • 2026-08 · JianYing (CapCut CN) export. The final film becomes an editable JianYing draft: per-shot clips, native caption tracks, separate SFX/BGM tracks. Verified on JianYing Pro 11.2 for macOS (guide).

❤️ Sponsors


APINEBULA

Thanks to APINEBULA for sponsoring this project! APINEBULA is an enterprise-grade AI aggregation platform operated by 银河录像局. Backed by its parent platform's resources, it provides stable, cost-effective access to large language model APIs for developers, teams and enterprises. Access full-capability Claude, GPT, Gemini and other leading models through one API, with model pricing starting at 6% of the regular price. Enterprise services include high concurrency, formal contracts, corporate bank transfers and invoicing.

Register through this link and enter the promo code video when topping up to get 10% off.

AWS

Amazon Web Services (AWS) offers reliable, scalable cloud computing services, including compute, storage and AI.

Explore AWS →

Install

Built and tuned for Claude Code and Codex. The simplest way is to hand your agent the link:

Install this skill for me: https://github.com/Vincentwei1021/video-shotcraft

Or with the skills CLI:

npx skills add Vincentwei1021/video-shotcraft

Or by hand:

git clone https://github.com/Vincentwei1021/video-shotcraft.git
cd video-shotcraft
ln -s "$(pwd)" ~/.claude/skills/video-shotcraft   # Claude Code
ln -s "$(pwd)" ~/.codex/skills/video-shotcraft    # Codex

In mainland China, clone from the AtomGit mirror if GitHub is slow: git clone https://atomgit.com/VincentWei/video-shotcraft.git.

Use

Just describe the film. No command needed.

Say What happens
Use video-shotcraft to make a promo for my product. The agent introduces the Ink Press template and asks whether to use it, then captures your pages and builds the film
Make a launch film for this repo with the Ink Press template. The fastest path: your screenshots, copy and logo dropped into a validated template
Use the deck-deal-flyin and row-embed shot cards to present this feature. You pick the shots by name (copy names straight from the Gallery)
Design a product close-up inspired by spotlight-hero-card. One shot, adapted to your product

Shot library

124 recipe cards in 10 categories, 150 shots in total. Search, filter and copy card names in the Gallery.

Opening & Brand · 11 shots

text-as-mask: the product shows through the title		 Camera · 13 shots

exploded-view: the page tilts and comes apart
Transitions · 19 shots

card-flock-tumble: a flock of cards becomes the headline		 Typography · 25 shots

flying-words: a word tunnel resolves into the motto
UI Entrance · 22 shots

card-stack: a fan of cards deals into place		 Interaction · 13 shots

palette-theme-ripple: a new theme ripples across the UI
Data · 9 shots

axis-rescale-shock: the spike breaks the axis		 Light & Emphasis · 23 shots

spotlight-sweep: a stage light finds the title
Rhythm · 8 shots

paparazzi-flash: three flashes, three crops, one number		 Outro · 7 shots

input-morph-assemble: the chat box builds the logo

Each card lives in references/shots/<category>/<card>.md, with its Remotion implementation in demos/<category>/<card>/ (see demos/README.md for how to wire one into your project).

Motion Workbench

After delivery the skill opens a CapCut-style editor in your browser (node workbench/scripts/open.mjs <project>). The film is split into shot, transition, caption and SFX tracks exactly as authored. Select any shot to edit its copy, font sizes and colours, move, trim or speed-ramp clips, drag in any of the 150 library shots, then export with Remotion. Preview and render are frame-identical.

Workbench guide, every panel with screenshots (Chinese) · Integration contract

What you get

Output Details
Final film MP4, 1920×1080, 30 fps, h264, with music and sound design
Remotion project The full source of your film: every shot is a React component you or the agent can change
Motion Workbench Opens after delivery: tracks, inspector, retime, swap shots, export (details)
JianYing draft Optional: an editable JianYing (CapCut CN) project with per-shot clips, captions and audio tracks
Social publishing Optional, when you ask: publish the finished film via Upload-Post to TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn, X and more. Confirm caption and platforms, then dry-run before posting (guide)

Also in the box: reusable Remotion components (2.5D page camera, captions, flash cuts, digit rolls), Freesound SFX search/download tools and 5 BGM tracks, page-capture scripts, and the production method itself (capture, visual direction, storyboarding, sound design, beat sync, final QA) in references/.

Showcase

Share your film. Made something with video-shotcraft? Submit it with the Showcase issue form. After review it appears on the Showcase page.

Requirements

Needs For
Node.js and npm Remotion rendering, the template and the workbench
ffmpeg / ffprobe Frame checks and final QA
uv Only for BGM beat analysis (runs a one-off Python script)
puppeteer Only for page capture; the capture script installs it on demand

Remotion downloads its own headless Chrome on first render. Tested on macOS; Linux works with the notes below.

Headless Linux / CI notes

Rendering on a headless Linux box (tested: 2 cores, Node 22) hits three walls:

  1. Concurrency cap. remotion still/render fails with "Maximum for --concurrency is 2" on low-core machines. Pass --concurrency=1.
  2. Old headless removal. Recent Chrome/Chromium dropped the old headless mode, so pointing Remotion at system Chromium fails to launch. Use a chrome-headless-shell binary instead of full Chrome.
  3. Blocked CDN. If remotion.media is unreachable (common in mainland China), the automatic headless-shell download fails. Pass --browser-executable=<path-to-local chrome-headless-shell>.

With these three flags, frame renders from the bundled template work.

Repository structure 
video-shotcraft/
├── SKILL.md                 # Agent entry point and core production rules
├── references/
│   ├── pipeline.md          # End-to-end production workflow
│   ├── shots/               # 124 shot recipe cards in 10 functional categories
│   ├── sequences/           # Reusable full-video structures and sequence patterns
│   ├── aesthetic-rules.md   # Visual QA criteria
│   ├── music-beat-sync.md   # BGM analysis and beat-sync methodology
│   ├── sound-design.md      # Sound-design guidance and examples
│   ├── sfx-sourcing.md      # Freesound search, download, analysis and credits
│   ├── jianying-export.md   # JianYing (CapCut CN) project-export guide
│   ├── publish-upload-post.md # Optional social publishing (Upload-Post API)
│   └── workbench.md         # Motion workbench: manifest contract + editability rules
├── demos/                   # Remotion reference implementations (same categories)
├── gallery/                 # Static motion-preview Gallery
├── template/                # Runnable complete video template
├── jianying-export/         # JianYing draft installers (mac tested / win untested)
├── publish/                 # Optional social publisher (stdlib-only Python) + offline tests
├── workbench/               # Post-delivery motion workbench (Vite + Remotion Player)
└── assets/
    ├── lib/                 # Reusable Remotion components
    ├── scripts/             # Page capture + Freesound CLI and offline tests
    └── audio/
        └── bgm/             # 5 BGM options; SFX downloaded per project

For the full workflow see SKILL.md, the production pipeline and the visual QA criteria.

Audio and assets

SFX come directly from Freesound, downloaded into each video's project. The shared SFX library has been removed. The sourcing guide covers search, CC0 / CC BY filtering, MP3 preview downloads, measurements and source/credit manifests. The Python CLI uses the standard library; downloading and analysis require FFmpeg. No API key is needed. Sound design covers timing and mixing. The template retains its fixed historical audio for playback and regression checks; new product videos source their SFX from Freesound. BGM options remain in assets/audio/bgm/.

Product screenshots bundled with the template are demonstration assets. Replace them with screenshots of your product before publishing, and check whether any product, customer or personal data needs to be anonymized.

License

  • Code and docs: Apache-2.0.
  • Freesound audio: each file under its recorded license; retain the project manifest and publish required CC BY credits.
  • BGM: see ATTRIBUTION.md. Historical template audio: see template credits.
  • Remotion has its own license: free for individuals and small teams, companies may need a paid license.

Acknowledgements

Many recipes were distilled by studying the motion language of outstanding official product films, including promos from ClickUp, Perplexity, Slack, Notion, Figma, Framer, Bear, Raycast, Pitch, Miro, Superhuman and Loom. The cards document techniques (timing, easing, choreography) re-implemented from scratch; no footage, artwork or brand assets from these films are included. All trademarks belong to their owners, and none of these companies are affiliated with or endorse this project.

The Freesound sourcing workflow was inspired by vibe-motion/sound. Thanks to its authors for sharing the approach of selecting sounds by source descriptions, duration, download counts, rating counts and licenses. Video Shotcraft's search/download CLI is independently implemented.

Thanks also to Remotion, which powers every demo and template here; Freesound and its contributors for project SFX; Mixkit for BGM and historical template audio; the game-feel and animation communities whose published principles inform several cards; and Claude Code, with which this library was built, iterated and QA'd using the same workflow the skill teaches.

☕ Support this project

If this project helped you, you're welcome to buy me a coffee and support its continued development and maintenance.

One-time tip on Ko-fi with a card or PayPal. In mainland China? Use WeChat below:

Scan with WeChat; any amount is appreciated. On a phone, save the image and select it from your album in WeChat's Scan feature.

Sponsorship is entirely optional. Stars, feedback, and sharing are just as welcome. Sponsorship does not change this project's license terms.

Follow me

Star history

💬 WeChat community

Join “Vincent 的 AI 交流群 3” to chat about AI applications, coding, and video creation.

Scan with WeChat to join. On a phone, save the image, then open WeChat’s Scan feature and select it from your album.

This QR code is valid before 2026-11-26, subject to WeChat’s notice. If it has expired, contact Vincent on X for the latest way to join.

item.title: JetBrains/thinkrail
item.description:
ThinkRail is the agentic IDE that gets better every time you use it

https://thinkrail.ai/

ThinkRail

ThinkRail is an agentic IDE that gets better every time you use it. With Spec-Driven Development support, it learns your project as you work, becoming more capable and helpful over time.

We built a rich interface around the pi coding agent, isolated work into separate workspaces, and gave the agent durable project knowledge through the spec graph and reusable skills. We are now adding full extension support, so ThinkRail can create the tools it needs based on how you work.

Website: thinkrail.ai · Blog: thinkrail.ai/blog · Discord: thinkrail.ai/discord

⭐ If you find ThinkRail useful, give it a star. It helps others discover it.

*From the left: An isolated workspace, a work session with an AI agent in that workspace, the code change made by the agent, and the spec tree.*

Installation

ThinkRail ships in two forms: a native desktop installer and the self-contained thinkrail CLI. You can install them from out Landing page.

For latest version, see the Releases page.

What you get

  • Isolated workspaces. Open any git repo as a project and create git worktree workspaces from it, each with its own branch and working directory. Agents can then work in parallel without touching your original codebase; when they finish, merge the results you want to keep and delete the rest. Ask a chat to do something "in a side workspace" and the agent starts that workspace and its chat itself, then checks how its chats and pull requests are doing. You can also attach existing git worktrees or explicitly work in the project folder.

    • Finished and dormant workspaces are settled when their pull request merges or closes, or after a quiet week, and return the moment you work in them again.

    • The topbar shows where the active branch stands against origin, and the state of its pull request. From there you can publish, push, or open a new PR described from the plan, the commits, your PR template, or an agent-written draft.

    • Once a GitHub PR is open, ThinkRail shows its CI checks and review decision, and lets you mark it ready, merge it, reopen it, or delete the remote branch.

  • An IDE around the agent. ThinkRail comes with Monaco editor tabs, a file tree integrated with git to show code changes as they happen, terminals, and document support. Rendered Markdown previews have a heading outline that follows the section you're reading; hide it or move it to either side. The pane you're typing in carries an accent line, a frame briefly lights the pane the keyboard takes you to, and VS Code-style keys move you around: F6 steps between panes, ⌘L jumps to the chat input, ⌘0 to Projects, ⌘1–⌘9 to an editor group, and ⌃` to the terminal; ⌘\ splits the editor and ⌃⌘← / ⌃⌘→ move a tab between groups. In a chat, ⌘↑ steps from the input into the conversation, where arrows or j/k walk messages, tool calls and thinking blocks, →/← unfold them, C copies and O opens the file a tool touched. When the agent asks a question, F6 (or ⇧Tab from the input) lands on its options, ←/→ page its questions and → past the last one reaches Submit, D marks it for discussion, I steps into an HTML mockup and ⌘↵ answers. Review comments need no mouse either: Tab onto a diff and a line cursor moves with arrows or j/k (h/l switch sides, Shift extends), Enter comments, and rendered Markdown blocks, image regions and the swipe divider take the same keys. Press F outside a text field (or ⌘; anywhere) for hint mode: every button, tab, row and field gets a short label, and typing it presses that element (Shift on the last letter only focuses it); Esc leaves a text field, so F works from anywhere, and repeated Esc climbs back to the main area; a waiting agent question takes focus unless you're typing. Switch hint mode off in Settings → Extensions & skills. In the sidebar trees S searches the visible rows and h/j/k/l move like the arrows. ⌘? opens a filterable, near-fullscreen cheatsheet of every shortcut in columns, with the pane you're in highlighted (a Mac browser keeps ⌘? for its Help menu, so use the keyboard icon at the bottom of the left tool rail or the palette there); tooltips show a button's shortcut. Settings works from the keyboard too: arrows move through the sections and the settings inside them, Delete resets a setting to its default, and S or / searches every individual setting. Rebind shortcuts in Settings → Keyboard, a tree of shortcuts by area that you can filter by name or by keys — the global chords and the keys a tree, tab strip, chat, review or palette takes while focused (letters like S, C or j/k, and chords like ⌘↵); arrows, Enter, Esc, Tab, Space, Home/End and PgUp/PgDn stay fixed. Bindings are saved on the host, so every window and browser follows, and export or import as a JSON file; extensions bring their own shortcuts, which you can rebind too.

  • Powerful chat features. You can open several concurrent work sessions per workspace, each with its own model. Send a prompt, or queue it as a follow-up, delegate to subagents, and work together on a shared plan: the agent updates it, and you review and edit. Settings → Subagents lists built-in, personal, and trusted workspace agents with their model policies. Switch individual agents off globally to block new launches without interrupting ongoing work, and set delegation and concurrency limits there.

  • Find anything from one box. ⌘K (or a double tap of Shift) opens a palette that finds chats and the messages inside them, workspaces and projects, files in the current workspace, specs, and plans, with a preview pane. It also runs the app's commands, including the active tab's layout commands (split, move to another group or pane, new or remove group, close), and opens Settings sections or an individual setting, and with nothing typed it lists the chats waiting for you. Type a task and press ⌘↵ to open Create workspace with it as the prompt. Press ⌘⇧F to find text inside the workspace's files as you type: matches are grouped by file, with match-case and whole-word toggles and a code preview, and ↵ opens the file at that line.

  • Chats without a project. Ask, plan, or draft without a repository. Each chat gets its own scratch folder under Chats for its files, terminal, and plan, with no branch, review, or pull request. Start one from the Welcome screen, the Create dialog, the palette, or the Chats section; deleting a chat moves its whole folder to the Trash. When a chat turns into work, Continue in workspace has the agent write a handoff summary and starts a new workspace chat with it.

  • Artifacts that stay. Everything the agent makes for you, such as design notes, mockups, diagrams, screenshots, and reports, lands in the workspace's git-ignored .thinkrail/context/ folder. The Artifacts tool opens on Outputs: just the finished files the agent published for you — the mockup, not its drafts and assets — the same files it hands you as clickable cards in the chat. Its Smart view groups everything it showed, linked or published, and the one you picked, with the scripts and scratch renders behind each folded away; List and Tree show every file, newest first or by folder. Each round in the chat lists the artifacts it made. It also names the chat that wrote each file and the ignored files its runs left behind. A dot on its rail icon tells you something new arrived. Nothing there disappears on its own: if the agent deletes a file, it stays listed, and opening it brings it back. The agent is steered away from leaving new files in /tmp. Mention an artifact in the chat, reveal it in Files, rename it, or cut and paste it into your project.

  • Always up-to-date specifications. A connected graph of SPEC.md files lives beside the code; the agent reads, searches, and maintains it through dedicated spec_* tools, so project intent persists across sessions. The read-only Specs tool renders the graph as a tree in its own view. Type # and a question in the palette to find the spec sections that answer it, in any word order and word form, ranked the way the agent's own spec_search ranks them. Press ↵ to open the spec at that heading, or ⌥↵ to ask the agent in a new chat when the specs phrase it differently.

  • Skills. ThinkRail loads your pi skills and any already in your project. It can also import skills from Claude, Codex, and other coding agents: switch them on in Settings → Extensions & skills, or per project in the Skills dialog, which also shows the size of your skill catalog. A large library is listed within a small prompt budget, and the agent finds the rest with a skill search.

  • Agent tools beyond the shell. Thanks to the ThinkRail GUI, your AI agent can ask you structured multiple-choice questions in the chat instead of guessing, draw Mermaid diagrams, and show comparisons and file previews. When the agent proposes a UI change, it shows a before/after mockup you can comment on like a diff; in a browser, the agent's mockups are clickable prototypes whose scripts run in a sandbox with no network access. Any HTML file, from a mockup to a generated report, opens in your browser from its tab, its preview or the Files menu. When a question's options come with mockups, open them full screen to flip through them, put two side by side (two HTML mockups scroll together and also compare with a swipe or an overlay), or see them all at once, and pick one right there. When it is done and waiting for you, it can suggest what you might send next as numbered one-click chips above the composer: ⌥1–⌥9 sends one from anywhere but the terminal, the code editor and dialogs, and Shift+click or ⇧⌥1–⇧⌥9 puts it in the input to edit first (both rebindable in Settings → Keyboard).

    • Settings → Extensions & skills lists the ThinkRail extensions the agent may use. It can also install any pi package by source (npm, git or a local folder), for you or for a repository, showing what each one adds and letting you switch individual packages, their extensions and skills, and pi's built-ins on or off.
    • The tools behind the questions, diagrams, previews, and next-message suggestions are also published as plain pi packages: pi install npm:@thinkrail/pi-ask-user-question for the questions (@thinkrail/pi-ask-user-question), pi install npm:@thinkrail/pi-visualize for the diagrams and previews (@thinkrail/pi-visualize), and pi install npm:@thinkrail/pi-next-steps for the next-message suggestions (@thinkrail/pi-next-steps, sent with Alt+1…9 in the terminal), so a vanilla pi in the terminal gets the same tools.

  • MCP servers. Connect the MCP servers in your pi mcp.json, or configure them in Settings → MCP servers. Your own servers, which apply to every project, can be added, switched on or off and removed there even with no project open. ThinkRail asks in the chat before calls that the server does not mark read-only, or always allows the tools you trust in a project. Servers a repository defines stay off until you approve them. ThinkRail signs you in to OAuth servers from Settings and shows each chat's servers next to its background commands and subagents, with each server's state and the chat's calls to it.

  • Your providers, your credentials. Sign in with JetBrains AI or connect any provider through pi's own auth. ThinkRail has no accounts of its own.

  • Your pi setup. ThinkRail reads your existing pi configuration (~/.pi/agent). To use another one (for example, a personal ~/.pi/agent-personal), or to pass extra environment variables to the agent, terminals and MCP servers, set them in Settings → Environment. The configuration becomes active on the next start. Settings → Models also holds pi's prompt-cache warming (off, only while a run is active, or also between runs); ThinkRail keeps it to active runs unless you choose otherwise, so idle chats don't spend in the background.

  • Your own model servers. Go to Settings → Providers → Custom servers and connect a company LLM gateway or a model running on your own machine. Any OpenAI-compatible server fits: LiteLLM, sglang, vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio, or llama.cpp.

    • The Find models button lists the models available on the server, together with their capabilities. The server is saved to pi's models.json. The models models appear in the chat model picker, and in the pi CLI alike.

  • Desktop app or browser. A native desktop app, or the thinkrail CLI that opens the same app in your browser. Both embed the same engine host. App state lives under ~/.thinkrail.

  • Your language. ThinkRail uses your system language or a language you pick in Settings → Language: English, Japanese, Polish, Russian, Simplified Chinese, Spanish, or Traditional Chinese (Taiwan). You can add a language ThinkRail doesn't ship yet by putting a translated locale file, for example de.json, in ~/.thinkrail/locales. (Tell your AI agent to do it for you!)

  • Your themes. In Settings → Appearance, you can choose from dark, light, minimal, and high-contrast themes. You can also make your own theme by copying a bundled *.theme.json, changing its id and colors, and saving it to ~/.thinkrail/themes. (Again, tell your AI agent to do it for you!)

  • Your fonts. In Settings → Text & fonts, you can pick the interface and code fonts and set separate line widths for chat and for code. You can choose from the bundled Geist and JetBrains Mono, any font installed on your computer, and font files kept in ~/.thinkrail/fonts, with fallback fonts for icon glyphs, a code size, ligatures, and a text-weight slider.

*The project's spec graph as a tree (on the right), with the spec itself rendered alongside in the center.*

Installation details

Desktop

Download the thinkrail-desktop-* asset for your platform:

  • macOS 14+ (Apple Silicon or Intel): open the DMG for your architecture: thinkrail-desktop-darwin-arm64.dmg or thinkrail-desktop-darwin-x64.dmg.

  • Windows x64: extract the complete setup ZIP, then run the executable.

  • Linux x64 / ARM64: extract the setup tarball and run installer. Desktop builds need glibc 2.38+ with GTK 3, WebKitGTK 4.1, Ayatana AppIndicator 3, librsvg 2, and Ubuntu 24.04 or newer, plus libnotify-bin for desktop notifications:

    sudo apt install libgtk-3-0 libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 libayatana-appindicator3-1 librsvg2-2 libnotify-bin

There are two update channels: stable and nightly. If the ThinkRail desktop app, you can check them in Settings → Updates: Download → Preparing update → Install & Restart.

Command line

The installer downloads the right binary, verifies its SHA-256 checksum, and puts thinkrail on your PATH.

macOS / Linux (also Windows under Git Bash):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash

Windows: the same command works from cmd and PowerShell:

powershell -c "irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex"

Then run thinkrail, optionally with a git repo to open as a project:

thinkrail ~/code/my-repo
  • thinkrail needs git on your PATH and a model provider. You can sign in with JetBrains AI from the app or use your own provider credentials. The first launch walks you through connecting a provider and picking a project; Start a new project creates an empty git repository (under ~/thinkrail by default), so you don't need one ready.
  • Add project → Clone repository… clones a Git URL into a new folder on the computer running ThinkRail and opens it as a project. Choose the parent folder and folder name, optionally limit the history depth, or cancel an in-progress clone.
  • GitHub and other Git hosts work with the Git credentials and SSH keys already on your machine.
  • thinkrail --help lists the flags, and thinkrail --version prints the build.
Nightly builds, pinned versions, updates, and uninstall The installer takes `--channel stable|nightly` and `--version`; a pinned version must belong to the selected channel: 
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel stable --version 0.3.1
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly --version 0.4.0-nightly.2

On Windows the options are environment variables (THINKRAIL_CHANNEL, THINKRAIL_VERSION, THINKRAIL_PREFIX, THINKRAIL_NO_MODIFY_PATH):

$env:THINKRAIL_CHANNEL='nightly'; irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex   # PowerShell
set "THINKRAIL_CHANNEL=stable" && set "THINKRAIL_VERSION=0.3.1" && powershell -c "irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex"   # cmd

If you keep ThinkRail running, it periodically checks for updates and, when it finds one, shows an "Update available" button in the GUI.

thinkrail uninstall removes the executable, the PATH entry the installer added, and the install metadata; it then asks whether to delete your ~/.thinkrail app state (kept by default; --remove-data deletes it, and -y skips the questions).

If you prefer a manual install, download a binary and the SHA256SUMS from the releases page, and verify the checksum. For self-update to work, rename it to thinkrail (thinkrail.exe on Windows) and place it at <prefix>/bin/thinkrail[.exe]; a binary kept under its release filename or elsewhere must be replaced manually or reinstalled with the script.

Platform notes

Platform Desktop CLI
macOS Apple Silicon / Intel DMG signed binary
Windows x64 signed setup executable and app binaries signed .exe
Linux x64 / ARM64 setup tarball, unsigned unsigned

JetBrains signs the Windows CLI, the desktop setup executable, and every executable and DLL the desktop app installs. The macOS CLI is signed but not yet notarized. Signed and notarized desktop DMGs must come from the coordinated JetBrains service pipeline; older published DMGs and locally built packages may still be unsigned and blocked by Gatekeeper. Linux artifacts are unsigned.

Analytics & privacy

ThinkRail apps collect basic usage events: launches, chat creation, message sends, and provider connections. The data is tied to a random installation ID. Usage analytics never include prompts, code, files, credentials, or account identity. Error reports are always sent as well, tied to the same installation ID, so we can fix crashes: they include the error type and code, and where in ThinkRail's own code it happened. They never include error messages, file paths, names, URLs, or anything from your projects or extensions.

Additional product usage is shared only while Share additional usage data is on; the switch is offered during first-run setup (or right after you skip it) and lives in Settings → Privacy. From the command line, thinkrail --no-analytics (or THINKRAIL_NO_ANALYTICS=1) turns additional sharing off for that launch. With additional sharing on, a packaged build may open the ThinkRail blog in your browser once to link your installation to the website visit that brought you here - only where you accepted marketing cookies on the website or no consent is required, and that link expires after 30 days.

Feedback surveys are separate from usage analytics. ThinkRail may invite you to a short survey, and you can also open it from Settings → Share feedback. Your answers, including anything you type, are sent to the ThinkRail team only when you press Send, and tied to the same random installation ID, not to your name or account. Please don't include secrets, code, or personal data. To have your answers deleted, email info@thinkrail.ai.

The ThinkRail apps and the ThinkRail website (thinkrail.ai) use PostHog Inc. services for analytics. The website also uses PostHog Surveys to collect feedback after a desktop download and, only if you choose to provide it, your email address, which is used to ask for further feedback and to send product updates. PostHog's privacy policy is at posthog.com/privacy.

Under the hood

ThinkRail is a thin host that runs pi in-process and bridges it to a web UI. pi owns models, skills, compaction, cost, and session state. ThinkRail owns workspace management, the GUI, and the contracts between the engine and the GUI.

  • Engine (packages/server + packages/shared): a Bun.serve HTTP+WS host with one in-process pi session per chat, launched by apps/cli or apps/desktop.
  • Contracts (packages/contracts): the typed, versioned protocol between the engine and the GUI.
  • GUI (apps/web): React 19 + Zustand + Tailwind v4, shipped independently; it communicates with the engine through the contracts.

goal-and-requirements.md and architecture.md are the product and design specs. ThinkRail is developed spec-first: a SPEC.md sits beside every module, and when a change made by an AI agent moves a boundary or a contract, the spec is updated in the same change.

Developing ThinkRail

You need Bun 1.4.4 (the pinned package manager and runtime), Node.js ≥ 22.23.4 (the in-process pi engine needs ≥ 22.19; the website build and typecheck need ≥ 22.23.4 for Astro 7.4), and an AI provider for agent work.

git clone https://github.com/JetBrains/thinkrail.git
cd thinkrail
bun install
bun run dev                          # host + web client together; Ctrl+C stops both

bun run --filter @thinkrail/cli dev  # browser launcher
bun run build:binary                 # standalone CLI artifact
bun run desktop:dev                  # package and open the Electrobun app
bun run desktop:build                # package without opening it

CONTRIBUTING.md covers the checks, the end-to-end suites, desktop packaging, and the repository layout.

Contributing

Contributions are welcome. See CONTRIBUTING.md. This project and community are governed by the Code of Conduct.

Community

Join us on Discord to ask questions, share what you're building, and talk to the team. Bugs and feature requests go to GitHub issues.

License

Licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

item.title: CopilotKit/OpenBot
item.description:
The open, self-hostable alternative to closed AI bots. Production-ready, fully customizable, and plugs into every stack: any agent, any model, any tool.

https://open.bot

OpenBot

AI coworkers. Ready for the enterprise.

A modular, self-hostable workspace for AI coworkers.
Choose your models. Bring your agents. Own your infrastructure.

open.bot · Docs · Deploy on Kubernetes · Run from source


Notarized .dmg for Apple silicon and Intel Macs · signed installer for Windows x64 · no terminal or developer tools needed · Release notes


From CopilotKit, creators of AG-UI.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c60f07da-8b6d-46eb-a573-17fc1e65a644

Watch a Bot use its browser and tools, answer with interactive results, and wait for your approval before it sends. Take over when it needs you, and connect the agents you already run.

Getting started

On your laptop

The easiest way to get started is with the fully self-contained app that runs on your laptop, combining the OpenBot frontend and Docker-based backend in one application.

Mac / Apple silicon · Mac / Intel · Windows

Run from source

For your team

OpenBot for Business brings your agents into one workspace with company sign-in, tool permissions, approvals, and audit. Deploy on your infrastructure or work with our engineers on hosting and customization.

Get early access to OpenBot for Business → · Talk to an engineer · Kubernetes setup

Web, mobile, and chat

Web · iOS · Android · Slack · Teams

Your workspace. Your stack.

  • Choose your models. Use OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, or open models through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, hosted by a provider or on your own infrastructure. Keep your provider relationships and change models as your needs change.
  • Bring your agents. Run built-in Bots in the OpenBot server, or connect your existing agents through AG-UI from any agent execution platform. Agents built with different stacks can work in the same workspace.
  • Make it yours. Use the MIT-licensed template as-is, white-label it, or customize it deeply. AG-UI connects agents, MCP connects tools, and the frontends and backend can evolve independently.
  • Govern work across your team. Company sign-in, roles, tool permissions, approvals, and audit apply across the workspace. Your agents use OpenBot's tools and computers under the same policies.
  • Get help deploying it. CopilotKit's engineers can work with your team to deploy OpenBot, connect your systems, and automate parts of specific jobs.

Connect your agent · Configure models and tools · Explore OpenBot for Business

Built on CopilotKit and AG-UI

OpenBot is built on CopilotKit, which is used in production by a majority of Fortune 500 companies.

Your agent stack. AG-UI has first-class integrations across the major agent frameworks and harnesses, including Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework and Agent Harness, Google ADK, AWS Strands, Oracle Agent Spec, LangChain, Mastra, Pydantic AI, Agno, and CrewAI. Many ship first-party support; Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supports AG-UI directly.

Your execution platform. Keep your agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Claude Managed Agents, Google's Agent Platform, LangChain's Managed Deep Agents, Microsoft Foundry Agent Service, or your own infrastructure. Connect them to OpenBot through an AG-UI endpoint, using an adapter where needed. Your choice of agent platform stays independent of your workspace.

Architecture

OpenBot has three parts. On your laptop, setup runs the backend and Intelligence for you. For a team, the Helm charts deploy both on Kubernetes in your own infrastructure: openbot-bundle installs the two together, and openbot installs OpenBot beside an Intelligence that already runs.

Part What it does
OpenBot frontends Mac, Windows, web, iOS, Android, Slack, and Teams connect people to the same workspace. Conversations, interactive results, computer view, and approvals adapt to each surface. Choose a frontend.
OpenBot backend Runs the workspace API and built-in Bots, connects external agents and tools, manages Bot computers, and enforces identity, permissions, action policies, and audit. Published as signed images and Helm charts, and reached through one API. Deploys on Kubernetes with PostgreSQL and persistent storage.
CopilotKit Intelligence Durable conversations, memory, Automatic Learning, and enterprise governance services. Separately licensed; runs on Kubernetes alongside OpenBot.

OpenBot enforces sign-in, tool permissions, action policies, and audit at its API, alongside Intelligence's platform services. Built-in Bots run in the OpenBot server; your own agents can run alongside OpenBot or on any agent execution platform. Both use AG-UI and can share the same workspace.

Computer execution is pluggable: use the default Kubernetes setup or connect a compatible external computer provider.

Architecture details · Services and ports · Kubernetes deployment

Open source, local operation, and licensing

The OpenBot application template is open source under the MIT license. You can fork, modify, and white-label it. It uses CopilotKit Intelligence, which is separately licensed and can run entirely on your own machine or infrastructure.

Where you run it CopilotKit Intelligence license
Your laptop, for personal use and experimentation Requires a free local Intelligence license. Desktop setup handles this for you.
Kubernetes evaluation Requires a free Intelligence trial license. Request a trial.
Kubernetes / production Requires a production Intelligence license beyond evaluation. OpenBot for Business includes Intelligence for use with OpenBot. Plans and pricing.

Fully local is an option. Run OpenBot, Intelligence, and a compatible model locally. A cloud model or connected online app still sends requests to that service. Initial downloads, account sign-in, and local license renewal need internet access.

Deploy on Kubernetes

Deploy OpenBot on AWS EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE, or your own Kubernetes cluster. Each release publishes two Helm charts:

Chart What it installs
openbot-bundle (openbot-bundle-0.1.0.tgz in v1.1.0) OpenBot and CopilotKit Intelligence together, on one PostgreSQL server. Nobody signs in to Intelligence: the chart makes OpenBot's organization, project and key in it. The quickest way to try OpenBot on a cluster, and the evaluation below.
openbot (openbot-0.3.0.tgz in v1.1.0) OpenBot alone, pointed at an Intelligence that already runs, managed or self-hosted: its two addresses in config.intelligence.apiUrl and config.intelligence.gatewayWsUrl, and a project key.

For a first evaluation, you need a cluster with a default StorageClass, kubectl, Helm, a trial or production license, and a model key. The install requests about 3.15 vCPU while it runs, plus about 0.4 vCPU while its install Jobs run; on EKS that is three t3.large nodes, not two. The commands below use an OpenAI key. For Anthropic, a model router, your own database, or OpenBot against an Intelligence you already run, use the Helm guide that comes with each chart (helm show readme on the chart).

Setting up with an AI assistant? Give it this README and the Helm guide (helm show readme on the chart below). The guide covers cloud-specific values, storage, secrets, sign-in, networking, upgrades, and troubleshooting. Use the evaluation below only through a local port-forward; configure sign-in and TLS before sharing a deployment.

  1. Create openbot-values.yaml locally. Replace the placeholders with your license and model key. Keep this file out of source control.

    openbot:
  config:
    singleUser: true
  secrets:
    licenseToken: "<your CopilotKit trial or production license>"
    modelApiKey: "<your OpenAI API key>"

  2. Install the openbot-bundle chart published with the release.

    This evaluation runs shared computers: every Bot runs on one computer, and a command one Bot runs can read another person's files. That suits a proof of concept only, and openbot.computers.sharedModeAcknowledged=true says you know it. For people, use sandbox mode instead, which gives each person a computer of their own and is more secure: install the agent-sandbox controller in the cluster and set openbot.computers.mode=sandbox (the Helm guide has the command).

    helm install openbot https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot/releases/download/v1.1.0/openbot-bundle-0.1.0.tgz \
  --namespace openbot --create-namespace \
  --values openbot-values.yaml \
  --set openbot.computers.sharedModeAcknowledged=true \
  --timeout 15m

    On arm64 nodes, add --set intelligence.embeddings.enabled=false. The OpenBot image runs on amd64 and arm64, but the embeddings server Intelligence runs for Memory is amd64 only. Without it, Memory recalls by keyword.

    From the release after v1.1.2, the chart also installs CopilotKit's management agent into openbot-system, which connects a team-licensed install to CopilotKit by default (see CopilotKit management). To leave it out, add --set openbot.management.enabled=false.

  3. Open your evaluation.

    kubectl -n openbot get pods,jobs
kubectl -n openbot port-forward svc/openbot-server 3001:3001

    Open http://127.0.0.1:3001. This configuration is single-user: anyone who can reach it is an administrator. Keep the port-forward local.

The chart generates every password, key and token both products need, creates both databases, and sets up Intelligence's organization, OpenBot's project and the Learning container. OpenBot's server migrates its own database as it starts and does the scheduled work itself, so there is no migration Job and no CronJob. Automatic Learning uses your model key too.

For OpenBot against managed Intelligence, or an Intelligence you already run, install the openbot chart instead (https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot/releases/download/v1.1.0/openbot-0.3.0.tgz) with config.intelligence.apiUrl, config.intelligence.gatewayWsUrl and secrets.intelligenceApiKey; its guide has the commands. A release of the 0.2 chart that still runs the Intelligence it installed is refused at upgrade to 0.3: keep it on 0.2, or install openbot-bundle as a new release in a namespace of its own.

For a team deployment, follow the Helm guide (helm show readme on the chart) to configure authentication, TLS, your database, secrets, persistent storage, and network policies. For a single-container alternative, see Deploy it.

CopilotKit management, on by default

From the release after v1.1.2, both charts install a management agent into the namespace openbot-system (management.enabled). With a team licence, the OpenBot server connects the install to CopilotKit's management service by itself, with no enrollment step. It never connects on OpenBot Desktop, on the personal edition, on OpenBot Cloud, or without a team licence.

  • What it sends. A heartbeat every minute over mutual TLS: OpenBot's version, chart and image digests, the last database migration, pod readiness counts, and upgrade state. No conversations, messages, files, prompts, names, secrets or logs.
  • What it does. It can restart a workload and write a support bundle to a volume in your cluster, on commands CopilotKit signs. It upgrades nothing until you set managed upgrades up, and then only in a maintenance window, after a verified backup.
  • How to turn it off. Set management.enabled=false (openbot.management.enabled=false on openbot-bundle), or have an admin press Disconnect on Admin → Managed updates. Connect there turns it back on.

CopilotKit management on Kubernetes lists every field that leaves your cluster and how to set up managed upgrades.

Run from source

Use the template to customize the workspace, branding, Bots, and skills. The source setup below uses an Intelligence on your own machine by default; managed Intelligence is the alternative.

git clone https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot.git
cd OpenBot

Requirements

To run the open-source template locally, you’ll need the following.

  • Docker, for PostgreSQL, the API server and the shipped Bots. The server and the Bots' computers run from the published OpenBot images, which scripts/start.sh pulls at the tag in backend-images.env: main in a checkout of main, the images built from main, and the release's own version in a release (v1.0.3 in the v1.0.3 tag). Nothing else is built or needed for them.
  • Bun 1.4+, for the app, the setup helpers and the tests (some tests fail on 1.3).
  • A CopilotKit account, for CopilotKit Intelligence. The free plan covers an Intelligence on your own machine and a managed project.
  • A model key. The example configuration uses OpenAI; Anthropic and Google work too, with BOT_PROVIDER set.

Quick start

The example configuration sets OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true, so you can try the app as a local administrator. Configure sign-in before giving anyone else access.

Setting up with an AI assistant? Paste prompt.txt into it first. It carries the same steps as below plus the things that are easy to get wrong: which of the blank keys in .env.example are actually yours to fill (the CopilotKit key and a model key), which the start script fills for you, and what each start-up refusal means. Every claim in it is checked against this repository.

  1. Create .env:

    cp .env.example .env
bun install

  2. Connect Intelligence. .env.example leaves its two addresses and its key empty, for one of these to fill.

    On this machine, the default (a preview for macOS with Docker Desktop; see Intelligence on your own machine):

    npx --yes copilotkit@latest login
npx --yes copilotkit@latest local setup
npx --yes copilotkit@latest local connect --approve-connection

    local setup installs Intelligence in a local cluster of its own, and local connect writes its two addresses and its project key to .env. Each installation has its own ports, which is why the example file has no address to ship.

    A managed project instead, where the local Intelligence does not run or to keep conversations in the managed service. Set the two addresses in .env first:

    INTELLIGENCE_API_URL=https://api.intelligence.copilotkit.ai
INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL=wss://realtime.intelligence.copilotkit.ai

    then:

    npx --yes copilotkit@latest login
npx --yes copilotkit@latest project select
bun scripts/setup-learning.ts

    login opens a browser on this machine. On a machine with no browser, such as over SSH, npx --yes copilotkit@latest login --device signs in with a code from a browser anywhere. project select asks which project in the terminal; where there is no terminal to ask in, name it: npx --yes copilotkit@latest project select --project <slug or id> --json.

    The helper provisions the selected project's runtime key, creates or reuses its openbot Learning container, then writes both settings to .env. It preserves custom container assignments and never replaces an existing OpenBot key; with one set, it only creates openbot in that key's project if it is missing. For fresh self-hosted setup, set INTELLIGENCE_API_URL to that deployment's HTTPS API origin (or http://localhost for a local one) and run the helper without the two npx commands. It opens an isolated Chrome or Edge window for your usual sign-in and project choice; install either browser first. For CLI-managed local evaluation installs, it discovers the matching dashboard with the newest installed or cached CopilotKit CLI and uses that dashboard for login and session requests. Discovery runs offline with Bun, without downloading the CLI or requiring npx on your PATH. If no CLI is available, manually hosted deployments use their API origin for sign-in. Complete the local auth approval shown in the browser when prompted. The runtime API URL stays unchanged. It writes the API URL, the key and the container, not INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL, so set that one to the same deployment yourself. Once openbot exists, the server assigns it as the default by itself unless Admin → Automatic Learning has a saved setting. Managed Intelligence needs no separate license token.

    The same CopilotKit CLI sign-in provisions Composio automatically when you run bash scripts/start.sh. If that cannot complete, OpenBot still starts, with apps unavailable. You can run bun run setup:composio first to prepare it separately, or later to retry; it does not need a Learning container. The helper creates or reuses one isolated Composio project for this installation and saves its project key to .env. Existing Composio keys and Arcade configurations are preserved. Keep the private .env.openbot-installation-id file across restarts and interrupted setup attempts; do not copy it into a new installation. This needs a published CopilotKit CLI with integrations composio provision and the hosted provisioning service enabled. See Composio setup for deployment preparation.

  3. Fill the remaining required values:

    • OPENAI_API_KEY, or for Anthropic both ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and BOT_PROVIDER=anthropic

    The example KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY is public and fine locally; generate your own with:

    openssl rand -base64 32

  4. Run:

    bash scripts/start.sh

  5. Open http://localhost:3010.

scripts/start.sh pulls the OpenBot images at the tag in backend-images.env, starts Docker services, starts the API server on port 3001 from the OpenBot server image (it applies its own migrations as it starts and fires routines itself), starts the app from this checkout on port 3010, and checks that the services answer their own health routes before printing next steps. It pulls on every start, so a checkout of main runs the images built from main now; offline, it uses the copies already on the machine. The server's log is docker compose logs server.

scripts/stop.sh takes the same things down, including each Bot's computer, which compose does not own; --keep-computers leaves the computers running. Nothing is deleted: the database, the Bots' files and their browser profiles are volumes.

On Windows

Run the clone inside WSL 2 with Ubuntu, and run every step above from an Ubuntu terminal. Windows (WSL 2) lists what to install in Ubuntu first. Keep an Ubuntu terminal open while you use OpenBot, and open the app from your Windows browser at http://127.0.0.1:3010. These steps were checked there with a managed project in step 2.

Intelligence on your own machine

The example configuration expects Intelligence on this machine, installed by the CopilotKit CLI as Evaluate Intelligence locally describes. The free Developer plan qualifies. The local license lasts 30 days and npx copilotkit@latest local renew renews it as often as you need, while your account is in good standing. It is a preview for macOS with Docker Desktop, not a production installation. Run its npx copilotkit@latest local connect from the OpenBot root, where .env is.

That command writes INTELLIGENCE_API_URL, INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL and CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY to .env. OpenBot reads those settings directly; no key copying or renaming is needed. INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY remains supported for older configurations. When both are set, the non-empty CLI key takes precedence so reconnecting uses the new project's key.

To give the Bots a Learning container on that stack, see Automatic Learning.

Deploy it

One image carries the app, the API, the browser the Bots drive, and optionally PostgreSQL. Same .env, no Kubernetes.

# The published image. Nothing to clone and nothing to build.
docker run -p 3001:3001 --env-file .env \
  -e EMBEDDED_POSTGRES=on -v openbot-data:/var/lib/postgresql \
  ghcr.io/copilotkit/openbot:latest

Everything is on 3001 here, the app included, rather than the 3010 the clone uses. latest is the most recent release and a version tag such as :v1.0.1 pins one.

Leave EMBEDDED_POSTGRES off and set DATABASE_URL to point at a database you already run. docs/deployment.md has the minimum sizes, the platform notes, and how it behaves behind more than one replica.

Try it

Pick a task you know well enough to review. For example, ask a Bot to check a hotel receipt against a travel policy in Drive. Have it show the room rate and tax separately so you can decide whether the claim meets the nightly limit. Use Teach a Bot to record the steps you want it to follow on the next claim.

  • Open /bot and ask: Open news.ycombinator.com and tell me the top story.
  • Ask the Bot to fill out https://httpbin.org/forms/post, then inspect /admin/audit.
  • Open /admin/boundaries, add a deny rule or preset, and retry the same browser action.
  • Create a Bot from /bots, give it a standing role, and start a channel with it.

What it is

In Personal Edition, you start with one assistant on your computer. With the source template, Docker Compose starts the supporting services, PostgreSQL stores the workspace configuration, and you choose the model. OpenBot encrypts stored model credentials and keeps them out of logs.

The team template comes with two Bots. General Assistant helps with everyday work. Knowledge answers questions from the company documents you connect and cites its sources.

To add a Bot, open /bots or start from one of the YAML examples. For example, Meeting Follow-ups reads meeting notes and lists who agreed to do what. Copy its file into examples/fintech/agents/ and restart OpenBot to try it. You grant tool access separately, so you can let a Bot read a document without giving it permission to edit it.

More at open.bot.

Built on AG-UI

A Bot is any endpoint speaking AG-UI, the open protocol for agent-to-user interaction, so OpenBot is not tied to a framework and neither are you. Agents built with LangGraph, Mastra, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Google ADK or written by hand all arrive the same way, and the governance rides the protocol rather than the framework.

Main surfaces

A Bot has eight things, always listed in this order: Conversations, Routines, Memory, Skills, Apps, Computer, Approvals and Activity. How OpenBot works explains each one. Each is set in at most three places: for one Bot on its page, for every Bot in the main menu (Routines, Memory, Skills, Connections) or Settings (the rest), and, in the team edition, for everyone in Admin.

One Bot Every Bot Everyone (Admin)
Conversations /channel/:id, /bot?agent=<id> /, /channel/new
Routines /bots/:id/routines /routines /admin/proactive
Memory /bots/:id/memory /memory
Skills /bots/:id/skills /skills /admin/skills, /admin/learning
Apps /bots/:id/apps /connections /admin/plugins, /admin/components, /admin/playground
Computer /bots/:id/computer /settings/computer /admin/computers
Approvals /bots/:id/approvals /settings/approvals /admin/approvals, /admin/boundaries, /admin/what-if
Activity /bots/:id/activity /settings/activity (personal edition) /admin/audit

Beside the eight:

Route Purpose
/bots Every Bot you can reach; create one, and open its page to change it.
/bots/:id One Bot: what it waits on you for, what it is doing, and its rows in the order above.
/bots/:id/setup The Bot's name, instructions and who it hands work to.
/bots/:id/reach, /bots/:id/sharing Team edition: reach the Bot in Slack, Microsoft Teams or by text, and share it.
/settings Your account and preferences.
/settings/notifications Where updates go, your devices, and recent deliveries.
/settings/vault Your saved logins and, in the personal edition, your keys. No Bot sees what is in it.
/settings/setup What OpenBot has and still needs.
/admin/credentials Admin → Vault: write-only encrypted credentials for the deployment.
/admin/people, /admin/permissions, /admin/identity-providers, /admin/providers Admin → Team: who can sign in, what they may do, and which models Bots use.

Old addresses redirect to the pages above:

Old address Opens
/capabilities, /capabilities/skills, /settings/skills, /settings/learning /skills
/settings/skills/new, /settings/skills/:slug (personal edition) /skills/new, /skills/:slug
/capabilities/memory, /settings/memory /memory, which opens /bots in the personal edition
/responsibilities /routines
/bots/:id/responsibilities /bots/:id/routines
/bots/:id/access /bots/:id/apps
/settings/passwords, /settings/credentials /settings/vault
/settings/credentials/new /settings/vault/new in the personal edition, /settings/vault in the team edition
/settings/this-computer /settings/computer#this-computer
/settings/browsers /settings/computer#browsers

Features

  • A computer per person: the supervisor gives each person their own container, with a folder and browser profile for each of their Bots. Tick Isolated on a Bot to give it a container of its own. Set COMPUTER_RUNTIME=runsc to run them under gVisor where the host supports it.
  • A shell, not just a browser: a Bot can run a command in its workspace, install what it needs, and process a file it saved. Through the same gate as everything else, so a rule can refuse a shell outright or refuse particular commands, and the command is on the record either way. The command inherits PATH, locale, terminal and proxy variables, not the rest of the deployment's environment.
  • The gateway is the only way in: it resolves the target from a server-held snapshot, evaluates the policy, writes the audit row, and only then calls the computer. There is no path that acts without the record existing first.
  • CEL policy, fail closed: rules can inspect tool.name, intent, bot.id, actor.id, page.url, page.host, element.*, key, command, file.*, mcp.* and initiator.* (what started the run, so a rule can refuse a scheduled routine what it would allow a person). Deny is evaluated before allow, a missing policy permits nothing, and a broken rule refuses rather than opens.
  • Watch what it is doing: the screen shows what a Bot is looking at, and the Activity list under it shows what it ran, read and saved in this conversation, with the output. A command line in the transcript opens to the same thing. A saved file shows its path and size, never its contents.
  • Take the wheel: a Bot that hits a login wall or a 2FA prompt asks for help. Control is handed over in the same panel and recorded as computer.help_requested, computer.control_taken and computer.control_released. While a person is driving, Bot actions are refused rather than queued.
  • Secrets never enter the transcript: the trail records that a secret was requested and how long it was, not what it said.
  • Bring your own agent: any AG-UI endpoint is a Bot, on a framework or hand-written. Endpoints are validated with the same target checks used for browser navigation, and an auth header is stored write-only.
  • Components instead of prose: compiled React components live in app/src/components/gallery/, sandboxed ones are authored in /admin/playground and published with no deployment. Every call asks the server whether the component exists, is published, and is not withheld from that Bot. Data functions are granted per component.
  • Governed MCP: Google Drive, Notion and the public-web research providers Parallel, Exa and Firecrawl ship in the catalogue, and Composio brokers a few hundred more apps behind one account (Arcade can be the broker instead), each reached as the person asking. The catalogue carries only vendors this deployment stands behind, so adding one is a review of that vendor. Custom servers must pass URL checks; unknown tools and custom-server tools are treated as writes, and a catalogue tool the server advertises but does not name as a write classifies as a read. A Bot is told which connectors exist here and which it holds, so it says it has not been granted one rather than browsing to the vendor's website.
  • Skills are instructions, not capabilities: personal skills attach only to Bots their author owns, deployment skills are admin-owned, and both are invoked with / in the composer. A Bot granted the shipped skill-creator skill can write one with you in the conversation, and saves it only when you press the button on the card.
  • Sign in with what your company already has: Google, Microsoft or Okta from the environment, or a company's own SAML or OpenID Connect provider registered while the deployment runs and routed by email domain. Any one turns sign-in on; several may be configured at once.
  • Decide who gets in: /admin/people lists everybody who has signed in, promotes and demotes them, and removes access, which ends the session they are using and stops the next sign-in. Every change is on the audit trail.
  • An audit trail you can read: /admin/audit lists what was permitted, what was refused and what failed, and every refusal carries the rule that caused it.
  • Credentials encrypted at rest: stored through /admin/credentials, never returned by an API, and redacted from audit events.
  • Loopback by default: computers bind to 127.0.0.1 and require a per-container token, so nothing reaches a logged-in browser by knowing its port. The supervisor binds there too, because it holds the Docker socket and its token is a shared secret rather than a network boundary.
  • Durable threads and memory: conversations survive restarts through CopilotKit Intelligence, and each deployment stamps the threads it owns.
  • Routines: ask a Bot to do something on a schedule and it does, running as you, in the channel you asked in. A 15-minute floor and a cap of 20 enabled routines keep a sentence from scheduling more than a person meant, and ten failures in a row switch a routine off rather than burn model spend forever. The server fires them itself, so there is nothing else to run; see docs/routines.md.

Bring your own agent

Any AG-UI endpoint can be a Bot.

From /bots, create a Bot with:

  • name and instructions, which become its role description;
  • private or public visibility;
  • optional AG-UI endpoint, with the framework the agent is built on when it is one New Bot lists;
  • optional write-only authorization header.

The server validates agent endpoints with the same target checks used for browser navigation, at registration and again on every redirect the endpoint answers with. If no custom endpoint is set, product-created coworkers use MANAGED_AGENT_AG_UI_URL when it is configured, and otherwise run in the OpenBot server on their role description.

A private address is refused unless it is listed in AGENT_ENDPOINT_ALLOWED_HOSTS:

AGENT_ENDPOINT_ALLOWED_HOSTS=agents.internal,10.0.0.42:9000

A host on its own covers any port on that host; a host with a port pins that port. Matching is exact: no wildcards, no suffixes. An entry written as a URL, or containing *, stops startup and names that entry.

The list covers agent endpoints only. Browsing is unaffected, the addresses holding a deployment's own cloud credentials are refused whatever is listed, and listing an address permits registering an agent there rather than granting that agent anything.

Tenant package agents are declared in the package's own agents.yaml, in the directory TENANT_PACKAGE_DIR names (examples/fintech by default), or each in a file of its own under that package's agents/ directory, as one of:

  • built-in, with a system prompt;
  • remote-ag-ui, with an endpoint; or
  • remote-mastra, with a Mastra server's address.

See docs/configuration.md and docs/coworkers.md.

Configuration

.env.example is the source template. The API server refuses to start without:

  • DATABASE_URL
  • KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY
  • INTELLIGENCE_API_URL
  • INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL
  • CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY (or the older INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY)

COPILOTKIT_LICENSE_TOKEN is optional. With none, the server starts on the Intelligence project key, once the Intelligence at INTELLIGENCE_API_URL accepts it; managed Intelligence issues no license.
