  • codex is the one client a plugin install cannot make self-sufficient: codex routes model traffic via env only (no config-file routing seam for the default ChatGPT-login provider — a managed model_providers block would force API-key auth and drop subscription login), and an MCP server cannot inject env into its parent. bili plugin install codex writes a single [mcp_servers.bili] block into ~/.codex/config.toml (command = node, args = dist/mcp.js) exposing the four ACP tools; at session start the shell resolves a proxy — env BILI_MCP_PROXY > the live-instance record (any lane's proxy or a bili start daemon) > the 8787 user-zone default (#1660 removed the install-time origin bake, #403) — nothing reachable → tools/list fails with -32003. So: start bili first (bili start or any client's lane proxy), export HTTPS_PROXY yourself if you also want compression, or use bili codex for the zero-config full posture. Mechanics: docs/clients.md.
  • claude has a native posture (#964): managed settings block + SessionStart hook + MCP shell; the hook rides the self-managed port zone (#1660) and re-pins the managed URL to the live origin each session, so port drift self-heals. Since #1821 the MCP shell also watches the proxy mid-session (30 s tick × 3 failures) and respawns a dead lane proxy itself, so model requests recover within ~90 s instead of a new session (same semantics as the zcode lane). Opt out with BILI_NATIVE_CLAUDE=0 (passthrough). Mechanics: docs/technical-notes.md. Known limitation (#2290): the Claude Desktop app's Code tab (CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT=claude-desktop) sets its own ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL on its embedded Claude Code, overriding the managed one — desktop sessions bypass the proxy entirely while the managed block's DISABLE_AUTO_COMPACT=1 still applies, so they get neither bili compression nor native auto-compaction. The hook warns loudly at session start (and records it for bili doctor, which also flags machines where Claude Desktop is installed alongside the native lane); terminal sessions are unaffected. Field-tested 2026-10-06 (#2290): putting HTTPS_PROXY in the settings env block produced zero CONNECT traffic to a live MITM-enabled proxy on Claude Desktop 2.19675.1 / embedded CC 2.1.288 (Windows 11) — the variable reaches no network stack there, matching the CLI behavior of that era — note that newer builds (CC 2.1.301+) DO honour HTTPS_PROXY on the CLI, which is why bili claude routes via the /bili/ base-URL rewrite — the launcher gives this lane no proxy and no CA at all, and a child that brings a proxy of its own gets the loopback hosts merged into NO_PROXY/no_proxy so that leg stays direct regardless of its proxy behavior (#3446). As of that version there is no usable routing seam on the desktop Code tab; the lane stays tracked in #2290 in case upstream changes behavior. Account-bound features (#4693): because the lane routes via a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, Claude Code treats the session as third-party/API-key and disables features bound to your Anthropic account/Cloud — Remote Control (/remote-control, driving a local session from mobile/desktop/web) disappears from the command list while bili routes traffic. Compression is unaffected; run plain claude without bili (or bili plugin remove claude) for sessions that need those features. This is inherent to the base-URL routing seam — no alternative interception point survives CC's undici stack (#2290) — not a config deletion. Desktop-only users can restore native auto-compact with bili plugin remove claude. Since #5095 the managed block also installs a SubagentStart hook (node <root>/dist/claude-subagent-hook.js) that mints a per-dispatch lane token into each subagent's context: subagents that ride the parent's session id with no agent-id headers (the VS Code extension build, #4352) key onto their own <id>|sub:…:t:<token> compression lanes, so parallel same-type dispatches stop merging (and the token disappears from later requests once the first message folds — those fall back to the fingerprint lane). Uninstall removes the hook with the managed block.
  • zcode has a native posture (#1145): managed ~/.zcode/cli/config.json block + per-session provider baseURL rewrite. Full mechanics: docs/clients.md.
  • jcode and aider have no native mode (no plugin/MCP/tool-injection seam: #962, #1048) — use bili jcode / bili aider.
  • copilot, amp and goose are launcher-only (#1049); goose cannot be cert-MITMed (rustls trusts no CA file) and rides plain-HTTP base-URL redirects instead.

Option 2 — Launcher (bili pi / bili codex / bili claude / bili omp / bili opencode / bili hermes / bili dsh / bili codebuddy / bili qoder / bili trae / bili jcode / bili kimi / bili gemini / bili iflow / bili qwen / bili antigravity / bili mcode / bili aider / bili copilot / bili amp / bili goose / bili kiro)

The launcher wraps a client in one command: it starts a proxy on an independent port (a fresh instance is always spawned — a port is never reused), then points the client at it — certificate-based MITM where the client honors proxy/CA env vars, or an isolated /bili/ config rewrite where it doesn't. No real config file is ever edited; the client's own config is READ to discover which HTTPS upstream hosts it talks to, and those hosts are whitelisted for MITM so the proxy can TLS-terminate exactly them and blind-tunnel everything else.

bili pi                               # launch pi through the proxy — file-free (#535): env + extension registerProvider, real ~/.pi untouched
bili codex                            # launch codex through the proxy
bili claude                           # launch claude through the proxy
bili omp                              # pi-style, file-free (#535): env + extension registerProvider + compaction cancel, real ~/.omp untouched
bili opencode                         # OpenCode (1.x & 2.x): full guide in the [OpenCode](docs/clients.md#opencode) section below
bili hermes                           # file-free (#535): hermes proxy env (HTTPS_PROXY + combined CA bundle via SSL_CERT_FILE) — https via CONNECT MITM, http via absolute-form forward proxy; real ~/.hermes untouched
bili dsh                              # deepseek-harness: full native plugin injected via --patch (#941) — real dsh tools, session-bound /acp + /acp-cache (plugin mode); non-loopback upstreams ride proxy envs, loopback keeps the overlay DSH_HOME rewrite (#535); dsh auto-compaction off everywhere — host plane via the bundle patch, web-profile presets at load time (#1772/#2474/#3354)
bili codebuddy                        # Tencent CodeBuddy Code CLI: CODEBUDDY_BASE_URL /bili/ rewrite (OpenAI chat completions wire), budget aligned via CODEBUDDY_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW; real ~/.codebuddy untouched
bili qoder                            # qoder CLI (`qoder`/`qodercli`): model endpoint is hardcoded https (no /bili/ rewrite possible) — cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, default model hosts whitelisted (#653). Qoder Desktop is a separate BYOK/custom channel that speaks plaintext OpenAI over a `/bili/` prefix — point it at bili as a normal custom provider (not this MITM lane); its official-subscription traffic is encrypted and out of scope (#764)
bili trae                             # Trae CLI (ByteDance, closed Go binary, no base-URL override) — cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + SSL_CERT_FILE, model host from TRAE_CLI_API_HOST or the default enterprise gateway (#655)
bili jcode                            # jcode (Rust agent harness) — env-only cert-MITM launch: HTTPS_PROXY + SSL_CERT_FILE, model host api.z.ai whitelisted, local loopback providers stay direct via NO_PROXY
bili kimi                             # Kimi Code CLI (Moonshot): standard proxy envs except an unconditional loopback bypass — https via cert-MITM, http via absolute-form forward proxy; loopback endpoints inventoried with a manual /bili/ hint (#757)
bili gemini                           # Gemini CLI (Google): GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL /bili/ rewrite to generativelanguage.googleapis.com (Google native wire), real ~/.gemini untouched
bili iflow                            # iFlow CLI: IFLOW_BASE_URL /bili/ rewrite to apis.iflow.cn/v1 (OpenAI chat-completions wire), real ~/.iflow untouched
bili qwen                             # Qwen Code (multi-protocol gemini-cli fork, no base-URL hook): cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, default DashScope/Qwen model hosts whitelisted, custom relays via --mitm-domain
bili antigravity                      # Antigravity CLI (agy, Google): CLOUD_CODE_URL /bili/ rewrite of daily-cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com — the real default upstream (bare cloudcode-pa 400s on /v1internal:*, #3129); undocumented language-server env override, v2.19.1 binary-verified; wire recognized as Google native by path (#2115)
bili mcode                            # MiniMax Code CLI: same shape as kimi (proxy envs, unconditional loopback bypass, cert-MITM/absolute-form); session bound via X-Mavis-Session-Id (#1050)
bili aider                            # Aider (Python pair programmer): cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + SSL_CERT_FILE/REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE; endpoint from OPENAI_API_BASE / ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL / --openai-api-base / .aider.conf.yml (#1048)
bili copilot                          # Copilot CLI (GitHub, closed Go binary) — cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + SSL_CERT_FILE, api.githubcopilot.com + per-plan subdomains whitelisted (#1049)
bili amp                              # Amp CLI (Sourcegraph, closed Go binary) — cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + SSL_CERT_FILE, ampcode.com whitelisted (#1049)
bili goose                            # Goose (Block, Rust/reqwest): rustls release builds trust no CA file — openai/anthropic legs via OPENAI_HOST/ANTHROPIC_HOST, custom providers via a regenerated GOOSE_PATH_ROOT overlay (/bili/ rewrites, real config untouched) (#1049)
bili kiro                             # Kiro CLI (AWS): cert-MITM via HTTPS_PROXY + combined CA on SSL_CERT_FILE and NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS; only runtime.<region>.kiro.dev is decrypted; developer/system items re-voiced as user for the gateway; session = Kiro's conversation id (survives --resume)
bili pi --mitm-domain api.foo.com     # add a domain to the MITM whitelist

Option 3 — URL change (/bili/ prefix)

Start the proxy:

bili

Then just prefix your client's existing baseURL with http://localhost:8787/bili/. The full upstream URL is embedded in the path, so the proxy knows where to forward without any config:

client baseURL before:  https://api.openai.com/v1
client baseURL after:   http://localhost:8787/bili/https://api.openai.com/v1

For more per-client configuration examples, see the web UI guide at http://localhost:8787.

Verify. With the proxy running and your config saved, check it answers and that your first real request shows compression activity in the log:

# Health check (proxy up + where it forwards)
curl -s http://localhost:8787/__bili/health
# → {"ok":true,"upstream":"https://api.anthropic.com"}

# Live session stats (after a real request)
curl -s http://localhost:8787/__bili/stats

Then send one message from your client and watch the log (~/.local/state/billion-context/bili.log, also printed to stderr). You should see a processTurn line per request, and once the conversation grows, [acp-usage] round N input=X cached=Y (cache hit Z%) + a compress event.

Client deep dives

Everything that doesn't fit in one Quickstart line — how each client's lanes attach, what gets written where, and known limitations — lives in docs/clients.md: dsh · Kimi Code · Hermes · ZCode · Gemini family (Gemini CLI / iFlow CLI / Qwen Code / Antigravity) · cert-MITM clients that never compress (CONNECT blind tunnels, #897) · unrecognized endpoints going direct (#1290) · OpenCode (launcher / native / pure proxy, /acp status & rules, legacy opencode-acp sessions #920).

From source (development)

Risk: master is the development branch and can be broken at any moment — unreleased changes, failing builds, unverified fixes. Unless you are patching the code or testing an unreleased fix, install a release with npm as above.

git clone https://github.com/ranxianglei/billion-context.git
cd billion-context
npm ci
npm run build
npm link
bili --version

After npm link, bili works from any directory.

FAQ

How do I check my cache hit rate? Don't dig through logs — /acp-cache prints a text summary report right in the client, headed by a clickable Web UI link: open it for the web version of the session page — the cache hit-rate line chart plus per-break attribution:

The report has four blocks that pin things down at a glance: GRAND LEDGER (totals + hit% with an explicit HEALTHY verdict; misses decomposed into new content / compress re-pay / upstream-ttl-or-client-rewrite) · FOLD ECONOMICS (per-fold economics: net tokens saved, paid-back verdicts) · LINE ITEMS (anomalies only: hit<85% or miss≥5000). Rule of thumb: compression itself costs ≤2% — a healthy session sits at 96–99%. When you see less, the attribution tells you which of the usual suspects it was, in this order: ① upstream cache TTL expiry (shows up as stable-prefix misses — the top-spikes line names idle times), ② a model switch, ③ a bili bug (report it with the page attached), ④ other/unknown. /acp-cache [full] lists every fold & line; same report over Since #1535 the report ends with a MODEL SWITCHES section: a mid-session model change invalidates the provider's prefix cache, so the whole stable prefix is re-billed on the next request — each switch's unexplained residual (its ttl bucket minus new content) is charged to the switch instead of masquerading as TTL expiry; per-event from → to, hit %, and attributed tokens are listed (full lists every event, the summary the last 8), and the web sessions table gains a matching model-switch column. Since #2131 the same machinery fingerprints the outbound credential (a 12-hex sha256 of the authorization/x-api-key-family headers — the raw key is never stored) and attributes a key switch — the relay behind a stable URL rotated to a different account — in a dedicated KEY SWITCHES section, a key switch: line in CACHE INVALIDATION, and a 🔑 badge in the web sessions column. HTTP: GET /__bili/cache-report; the raw per-request [acp-usage] lines still land in the log file for deep dives.

What does /acp show? In clients with the native plugin (opencode, dsh, hermes), /acp renders the ACP status panel of the current conversation straight from the proxy (session, blocks, compressible ranges, usage); before the first model request it shows an idle notice instead. /acp-cache [full] prints the cache report above.

Can I query sessions and config over the web? Yes — open http://localhost:8787: an overview dashboard, session list with per-session detail, live logs, a config editor, and an upstream connectivity test. A Blog view renders notes and long-form articles inside the panel itself — bundled with the install, refreshed from GitHub master on a ~1-hour throttle while online (fail-soft to the bundled copy when offline); the full library also lives on GitHub Pages. Everything else is also plain JSON for scripting (/__bili/stats, /__bili/sessions, /__bili/config, …).

When does compression happen? It is model-driven: the injected context tools are called by the model as context grows, gentle growth nudges (~50K-token steps by design, adjustable via compress.nudgeGrowthTokens) prompt it along the way, and preflight fires as a hard backstop when the input alone exceeds the window (#470). Watch it live with /acp or the web UI.

Does compression shrink my client's own conversation file? No — the most common surprise in very long sessions (#5796). Compression shrinks what is sent to the model: every outgoing request is rebuilt from live blocks plus summaries, so the wire stays small however long the conversation runs. The client's stored history is user data — bili never rewrites it. On dsh the host's auto-compaction is additionally disabled while bili is active (two compressors must not fight over one history, #1772/#2474/#3354), so the host-side file grows with every turn: each turn takes longer as it grows (measured: tens of seconds per turn at ~30K messages, #5796), and the practical convergence path is to start a new session when it gets heavy. The web session list badges sessions at 5,000+ requests (长会话/slow) as a reminder that this point has been reached.

Why does the first compaction wait until ~200k? Compaction does not trigger on absolute window position but on growth intervals: by default the first soft compaction fires 50k tokens past the boot content (compress.nudgeGrowthTokens, flat and window-independent). With a boot around 100k — or with the growth step set to ~100k — the first compaction may wait until ~200k. To make it fire earlier: 1) trim the system prompt, disable unneeded tools, prune skills; 2) lower compress.nudgeGrowthTokens to ~50k; 3) enable lean mode. Worked example in docs/configuration.md.

Is bili transparent? How do I turn it off? Unrecognized endpoints forward unchanged (docs/clients.md), and every mode reverses cleanly: bili plugin remove <client> for native installs, stop using the launcher command / env vars / /bili/ prefix for the other two — traffic goes direct again immediately.

Can I combine bili with a model-routing gateway (e.g. magpie)? Yes — point the client at bili, and point bili at the gateway through the /bili/ prefix, which embeds the gateway's absolute URL: http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425…. Example: Claude Code → ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425 + ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=magpie; OpenAI-style clients → OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1 (+ OPENAI_API_KEY=magpie). Compression happens before routing — every request that reaches any account in the gateway's routing groups is already compressed. Credentials stay in the gateway: the client's dummy key rides through untouched, and real keys never touch bili. Caveats: ① an account switch mid-conversation invalidates the provider's prefix cache — inherent to multi-account routing, not bili (watch it in the KEY SWITCHES section of /acp-cache); ② routed model names are opaque to bili's window lookup — declare their context windows under the providers key http://127.0.0.1:3425 via models.<name>.context, or they run on the fallback window (route-miss warning, #2317); ③ if the relay rejects bili's Anthropic-lane cache_control stamps, set compat.noCacheControl; ④ loopback gateways work out of the box; a gateway on a private non-loopback address may additionally need network.allowPrivateHttpProviders (#2984); ⑤ for Claude Code native plugin mode (bili plugin install claude), set BILI_CLAUDE_UPSTREAM=http://127.0.0.1:3425 before install so the managed block wraps the relay into ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL (or configure ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425 directly; localhost and 127.0.0.1 both accepted, #5369). Verified end-to-end over all three wires (OpenAI Chat / Responses / Anthropic Messages, including cross-protocol conversion), #4433.

Does this work with opencodex (ocx) — the local Codex/Claude Code gateway with a ChatGPT account pool? Same pattern: point the client at bili, and point bili at ocx through the /bili/ prefix — OpenAI-style clients (chat completions and Responses, e.g. Codex) → OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:10100/v1; Anthropic-style clients → ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:10100. A dummy key value satisfies clients that require one; it rides through untouched. Keep bili in front of ocx rather than behind it: ocx owns the provider credentials and the account pool at its final hop, so only this order keeps compression and pooling working together. Loopback needs no key between the two (ocx's default loopback bind reads no token); a non-loopback bind takes OPENCODEX_API_AUTH_TOKEN plus the x-opencodex-api-key header per its docs. Request models by ocx's provider/model id so routing is deterministic; as with any gateway, routed ids are opaque to bili's window lookup (declare them via models.<name>.context) and a mid-session account rebind invalidates the prefix cache (watch KEY SWITCHES in /acp-cache). Verified end-to-end over all three wires (OpenAI Chat / Responses / Anthropic Messages), bili 0.1.212 × ocx 2.97.0.

Where are logs and session data stored? Log: ~/.local/state/billion-context/bili.log (also mirrored to stderr); session state: ~/.local/share/billion-context/ (XDG-overridable; Windows AV exclusion #362, opt-in cleanup #1082) — full paths in docs/configuration.md.

Running the proxy

Running in Docker

A Dockerfile ships at the repository root — it installs the published npm package at build time (the tested artifact; nothing is compiled in the image) and runs the proxy as a service:

docker build -t billion-context .
docker run -d --name bili -p 8787:8787 \
  -v bili-config:/root/.config/billion-context \
  -v bili-data:/root/.local/share/billion-context \
  -v bili-cache:/root/.cache/billion-context \
  -v bili-state:/root/.local/state/billion-context \
  billion-context

Then point clients' baseURL at http://<host>:8787/bili/… exactly like Option 3 above.

  • Base: node:24-slim — uses the builtin node:sqlite storage engine directly (no native-addon download). Don't switch to Node 20 bases: the self-downloaded SQLite engine requires Node ≥ 22 and crashes under 20 (#3341).
  • Updates: in-container self-update is off by default (ACP_AUTO_UPDATE=0) — the sanctioned update channel for a containerized copy is rebuilding/pulling a newer image; an in-place self-update would be silently reverted to the image version on the next recreate. Opt back in with -e ACP_AUTO_UPDATE=1; pin a release at build time with --build-arg BILI_VERSION=0.1.197 (default latest).
  • Data: the four mounted dirs hold config, session state, update throttle/lock + cached SQLite engine, and logs respectively. Mount volumes or bind mounts so they survive container replacement; the image also declares them as VOLUMEs so even a bare docker run keeps them out of the container layer.
  • Security: the container listens on 0.0.0.0:8787 so clients outside it can connect — there is no authentication, so expose the port only on a trusted network (same caveat as --host 0.0.0.0 below). The web UI and /__bili/* JSON endpoints work unchanged through the mapped port.
  • Healthcheck: the image ships a HEALTHCHECK probing /__bili/health on 8787 via node's builtin fetch (no curl needed in the slim base); if you override the listen port, remember the probe stays pinned to 8787.

Flags

bili --port 9000              # change listen port
bili --host 0.0.0.0           # listen on all interfaces (see host note below)
bili --debug                 # verbose logging (also: set "debug": true in config)
bili --passthrough           # forward without compression (smoke-test mode)
bili --config ~/my-bili.json # use a different config file
bili -c dsh-test             # named config → ~/.config/billion-context/dsh-test.json (per-model files)
bili update                  # check & install a newer version now (bypasses throttle)
bili doctor --fix            # converge drifted dsh profile ledgers (manifest spec / lockfile record / bundle copy) to the on-disk version (#3496)
bili --no-auto-update        # disable self-update for this run
bili --auto-restart-on-update   # self-restart when a new version is installed (default off)
bili --bin /path/to/client   # launcher: spawn this exact client binary instead of auto-detecting (env BILI_CLIENT_BIN)

Flags override env vars and the config file. bili --help lists them all.

Remote agents (--host)

By default the proxy binds 127.0.0.1 and only accepts loopback connections. To serve agents on other machines: bili --host 0.0.0.0 (or your LAN IP); remote agents point their model baseURL at http://<this-host>:<port>/bili/….

  • MITM-mode CONNECT then also accepts remote clients — for whitelisted model hosts only. Blind tunnels to arbitrary hosts stay loopback-only, so the proxy can never be used as an open relay.
  • /bili/<absolute-url> destination admission (#409): the proxy itself and link-local/metadata addresses are always denied; loopback/private destinations are allowed for local clients (self-hosted upstreams) and denied for remote clients unless listed in BILI_TUNNEL_ALLOWED_HOSTS (host or host:port, comma-separated). One exception (#1073): a local client relaying a management path (/__bili/*, /__acp/*) to a loopback IP-literal destination is forwarded unmarked; remote peers and hostname destinations keep the internal tunnel marker unconditionally, and management paths stay unreachable through the tunnel even via NAT hairpin. An absolute-form request addressed to the instance's own endpoint on a management path is served locally instead of tunneled (a forward-proxy-style health probe gets a real answer).
  • There is no authentication: only do this on a trusted LAN or behind a firewall. The /__bili/ management endpoints remain loopback-only. A startup [security] warning reminds you of the above.

Debugging

bili --debug (or env ACP_DEBUG=1, or "debug": true in config — flag > env > config) logs every processTurn (tag counts, token usage), the nudge decision (growth/usage/pendingT1/shouldInject), client headers, and SSE rewrites.

Log file

All logs tee to ~/.local/state/billion-context/bili.log by default (XDG state dir) and still print to stderr. Override with "logFile" in config or ACP_LOG_FILE (off disables the file). Auto-rotates at 10 MB (bili.log.old). Per-request cache-hit stats log as [acp-usage] round N input=X cached=Y (cache hit Z%) so you can measure prefix-cache health directly from the log.

Connection lifecycle tuning (#1982)

Client-facing connections close gracefully after the final response: when the proxy initiates the close (Connection: close), it waits up to BILI_POST_RESPONSE_LINGER_MS (default 5000) for the client's close signal before releasing the socket, so pooled clients see a clean EOF instead of a possible RST from racing bytes. Related knobs: BILI_KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT_MS (idle-reap budget, default 5000) and BILI_CLIENT_ERROR_BACKSTOP_MS (terminal backstop for the error-drain path, default 30000) — full semantics in docs/configuration.md.

Self-update

The proxy checks npm on startup and every 3 minutes; a newer version is installed in place and a notice is logged — restart bili to pick it up, unless you enable opt-in self-restart (--auto-restart-on-update flag, env ACP_AUTO_RESTART_ON_UPDATE=1, or "autoRestartOnUpdate": true in config — default OFF): with zero in-flight requests it verifies the new install, stops accepting connections, drains, spawns a replacement on the same port, and exits once it accepts connections (clients reconnect automatically; session state survives on disk). Safety gates: zero in-flight through the drain window, an install sanity check before re-exec, and a 10-minute cooldown marker so a flapping version can never loop-restart; any failure resumes the original listener and falls back to the plain reminder.

Staggered rollout (#3619): a discovered version is not applied immediately by automatic updates. Each instance draws ONE random moment inside a delay window (built-in default 15 min – 48 h) and upgrades when it arrives; the drawn moment is persisted, so restarts never re-roll. Fleet upgrades therefore spread across the window instead of completing within minutes of a release, leaving time to catch a bad release mid-rollout (#3401/#3600/#3394). The window plus emergency controls live in a public policy file (auto-update-policy.json in this repo, fetched anonymously with ETag caching): hold freezes automatic upgrades fleet-wide, blocked skips listed versions, pinned sets an upgrade ceiling. Fail-open by design — an unreachable or malformed file simply falls back to local defaults, and the file can steer timing/skip/pin only, never what gets installed. Per-machine exits: manual bili update bypasses hold/stagger (still respects blocked/pinned), "staggerMinDelayMs": 0 + "staggerMaxDelayMs": 0 (or BILI_UPDATE_STAGGER_MIN_MS/BILI_UPDATE_STAGGER_MAX_MS) restore legacy immediate upgrades, and ACP_AUTO_UPDATE=0 disables auto-updates entirely. Full format and semantics: docs/configuration.md → update.

While the running process is behind the on-disk install ("stale"), the web UI shows a banner (running vs installed version, auto-restart state) and GET /__bili/status returns {version, diskVersion, stale, autoRestartOnUpdate, advisory, updatePolicy, inFlight} for scripting (advisory is the active critical-defect entry or null, see below; updatePolicy reports the #3619 rollout state — policy source, hold/pinned/blocked, and the pending staggered upgrade with its due time). Disable permanently via "autoUpdate": false in config or ACP_AUTO_UPDATE=0.

In plugin mode (bili opencode / bili pi / bili dsh — the proxy runs embedded in a long-lived host), "restart bili" means restarting the host: the embedded process cannot exit on its own, so a host left open keeps serving whatever code it started with, silently missing every fix auto-update reports as installed (#1603). Enable --auto-restart-on-update to have it self-restart at a safe point, or run /acp (OpenCode hosts today — pi/dsh coverage tracked in #2084) — the status panel appends a one-line staleness warning (running vs installed version) whenever the on-disk install is ahead of the live process. Auto-update only ever replaces disk files and (optionally) the proxy process; injected code inside the host process only takes effect after the host itself restarts — so if the injection breaks at runtime mid-session (a disposed agent scope, a disabled plugin), model traffic goes direct and uncompressed until then. Since #3581 this state is visible instead of silent: the web UI shows a "takeover broken" banner (agent + refusal count) whenever a plugin reports its attribution gate degraded while no session is live, and GET /__bili/status / /__bili/overview expose the per-agent attribution state (ok/none/threw, refusal count, first-refusal timestamp). Background lanes that are agentless by design (e.g. dsh's title-generation sidecar) never carry an initiator, so their small one-shot calls go direct by definition; under the #3651 contract these normal interceptions are NEVER reported and therefore can never raise the banner. The banner fires only when the attribution lookup itself throws (an internal host error, e.g. a disposed agent scope), and then names what failed: the thrown error text, the masked endpoint, when the episode started, how many requests went uncompressed, the remedy (restart the host process), plus copy/submit-diagnostics buttons that prefill a GitHub issue.

Update visibility is silent by default since v0.1.183 (#1977): routine/recommended releases no longer render an update line on the /acp panel footer or in acp_status — only a critical-tier release surfaces there (CRITICAL UPDATE READY/AVAILABLE). The standing ways to check an installed-but-not-restarted release are the stale cues above: web UI banner, the /acp one-line warning, and GET /__bili/status. Deliberately no always-on nag; the advisory channel (#1481) remains the only auto-visible critical path.

When an install keeps failing (unwritable or host-managed dir, network error, …), auto-update no longer re-downloads and retries on every 3-minute cycle forever. After three consecutive failures it backs off exponentially (5 min → 10 → 20 …, capped at 6 h), logs a one-time actionable hint (fix permissions / npm prefix, reinstall user-level, or disable via "autoUpdate": false / ACP_AUTO_UPDATE=0), and logs nothing further about the failure while cooling down (no download, no retry line); it resumes as soon as the failure clears or a different version is targeted (#1603).

The same bounded retry now covers the owner-managed lanes the global self-update drives instead of writing the copy itself — the dsh desktop in-place copy, the dsh profile bundles, and pi's npm copy (#2192). Each lane keeps its own failure streak keyed by lane + target version, so a persistently broken desktop layout no longer re-downloads the full tarball every cycle (up to ~480 downloads/day per affected machine before the fix); three strikes arms the same exponential cooldown, and the one-time hint names the failing lane and its manual fix (dsh plugin --profile <name> add …, pi update --extension …, or recreate the desktop profile). Host-managed instances additionally check on their own slower cadence — 30 minutes plus up to 15 minutes of jitter, tracked under a separate throttle marker — instead of consuming the global 3-minute budget. Failure streaks are shared across every bili process on the machine through a small state file in the cache dir (.install-backoff.json), so several running instances don't each burn their own retry budget; a clean bili plugin update disarms the dsh profile lane immediately. The file is written atomically (tmp+rename) and every writer merges with what is already on disk, so concurrent instances cooperate instead of overwriting each other's streaks; long-lived processes re-read it when it changes, so a manual disarm by one copy is visible to the others on their next check. It is fail-safe in the retry direction — a corrupt file or jumped clock is dropped, never allowed to silence a lane for long. bili plugin update clears the dsh-profile lane's key; a repaired desktop lane clears its own key on its next successful in-place refresh.

Stale local DNS after a network/VPN change (#5224)

A long-lived standalone proxy can keep holding stale OS-resolver state after a WSL/VPN/TUN topology change — the process caches its system resolver and libuv's getaddrinfo does not re-read /etc/resolv.conf on its own. Symptom: every model request through the /bili/ tunnel answers HTTP 502 tunnel_destination_denied with detail unresolvable, even though a freshly started bili resolves the same host fine at that moment and curl from a new shell works. Either remedy clears it:

  • Restart the proxy process — a fresh process re-reads the system resolver. In the launcher lanes and the dsh web-profile lane the proxy is a separate registered process (the instance registry), so restarting only the client/host re-adopts the same wedged proxy and does not help — you must stop and relaunch the proxy itself. (In embedded plugin mode the proxy runs inside the host, so restarting the host does clear it.)
  • Route egress through an upstream proxy — -F http://<host:port> or BILI_UPSTREAM_PROXY=… BILI_UPSTREAM_PROXY_MODE=auto: the destination is then resolved remotely by that proxy, so bili never consults its own (stale) resolver for admission.

Critical-defect advisories (forced updates)

Independent of auto-update (#1481): even with autoUpdate off, the proxy polls a small companion npm package (billion-context-advisories, published by CI from this repo's advisories/ directory) on the same 3-minute cadence. Each advisory names a semver range of broken versions (affected), the exact version to install (target — which may be older than the current one, i.e. a rollback), and a user-facing reason. When the local version falls inside affected, bili force-installs target through the self-updater's full safety chain (cross-process lock, backup + verify + rollback; source checkouts and host-managed installs are refused with manual instructions instead) and warns prominently: a one-time [advisory] ⚠️ … log line per process per advisory id, a banner on the web UI showing the reason and the exact manual upgrade command, and the active entry under advisory in /__bili/status. The check is fail-open by design: an unreachable or malformed advisory source only produces a warning — model traffic is never blocked by it. Disable via config ("advisoryCheck": false) or env (BILI_ADVISORY_CHECK=0); point at a custom document with "advisoryUrl" / BILI_ADVISORY_URL.

Announcements (#5548) — distinct from the defect advisory above, three sources feed the web-UI banners, and equal ids shadow in the order local file > remote feed > built-in: (1) built-in one-time notices rendered from the UI i18n strings; (2) local — drop JSON files into <config dir>/announcements/*.json (~/.config/billion-context/announcements/ by default) and they render automatically: bilingual records with kind-derived color, npm-style versions targeting (>=a.b.c, ^, ~, [lo hi], || lists), percent grey rollout, time windows, and per-kind priority — one bad file disables only itself; (3) remote — this repo's master branch announcements/remote.json (CI-linted on every PR), fetched on the ~3-minute watcher cadence, whose last-known-good snapshot survives restarts and outages while malformed pushes are rejected; unreachable installs (firewalls) point "remoteAnnouncementsUrl" / BILI_ANNOUNCEMENTS_URL at a relay mirror of the same document. Dismissal follows each record's declared mode: persistent (default, content-addressed — editing a notice shows it again), instance (this process run only), or always (renders without a close button). Dismissing a built-in intro notice is recorded per install in bili's unified storage (SQLite by default; the MySQL backend works too), so it survives restarts — the old upgrade-notices.json state file remains only as fallback on legacy-only installs without a unified sidecar. The official feed currently ships an empty entry list.

Configuration

The full configuration reference — config file location, top-level keys, providers, compression tuning, environment variables — lives in docs/configuration.md.

Config file

One JSON document at ~/.config/billion-context/billion-context.json ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/billion-context/; override the path with BILI_CONFIG_FILE; a bare name selects a sibling file, e.g. -c dsh-test → ~/.config/billion-context/dsh-test.json). Precedence when several sources set the same knob: CLI flag (where one exists) > env var > config file > built-in default — every env var keeps working as the override tier.

What's inside (details in docs/configuration.md):

  • providers — per-provider routing table: upstream override, model context windows, per-provider/model compress tuning, wire-protocol declaration, compaction opt-in.
  • compress — three-level compression tuning (global → provider → model): thresholds, nudge cadence, preservation rules, prompts, tiers.
  • Server-level blocks — process-wide behavior, including the #2030 additions: network (timeouts / retry / keep-alive / preflight cadence), persist (session persistence format + tail), sessions (cap + GC policy), update (registry mirror + check interval), diagnostics (dumps, render-tag mode, injection switches), fakeCompletion, plus scalars codexCompact / ccrRetrievalTtlMs / decompressTmpCap and extensions mitm.handshakeTimeoutMs, compat.noCacheControl, compat.keepResponseId.

Minimal example:

{
  "network": { "upstreamTimeoutMs": 900000 },
  "persist": { "zstd": true },
  "sessions": { "gc": { "enabled": true, "maxAgeDays": 14 } }
}

Knobs people look for first:

  • Upstream proxy (firewall/GFW) — routing the proxy's own outbound traffic through v2rayA/clash: full resolution order, empty-string = explicit direct, SOCKS5 rejection, both egress paths, and the mitm:// vs https:// key schemes live in docs/configuration.md (Server Settings → proxy; Providers → key schemes).
  • Wire-compat role rewrite (compat.roles) — an upstream that rejects the developer role? Covered by docs/configuration.md (Server Settings → compat) — including the learn-on-failure auto-fix that needs no configuration at all.
  • Signed upstreams (body-covering signatures) — a gateway whose requests carry a body-covering signature (CodeArts APIG's SDK-HMAC-SHA256, or gateway-invented headers like x-ofm-signature): the built-in scheme re-signs transparently on dsh; every other detected scheme is ALWAYS refused locally — signed requests are either re-signed+compressed or refused, never passed through unsigned — and bili keeps reminding at startup and in the web UI until it ships the scheme's re-signer (#1884/#2090). Detection rules, per-scheme overrides, and BILI_RESIGN / BILI_RESIGN_PASSTHROUGH / BILI_CODEARTS_REF live in docs/configuration.md (Server Settings → resign).

Pi built-in subagents

Using bili pi or the native pi plugin (bili plugin install pi) includes built-in subagent support, enabled by default: acp_delegate, acp_delegate_wait, and acp_delegate_cancel. This additional tool surface is specific to pi.

Keep only one subagent implementation enabled. If you use the built-in support, remove or disable other pi subagent plugins (for example, pi-subagents or a separately installed billion-context-pi-subagents) in both user and project settings to avoid overlapping tools, prompts, or behavior. If you prefer another subagent plugin, disable the built-in support instead. A pi-subagents install at either scope (project or user) makes the built-in delegate stand down automatically by default — a user-scope install loads in every project, so the guard applies there too (#5637); set delegate.forceEnable to keep acp_delegate alongside it.

To disable the built-in subagents while keeping context compression, merge this into ~/.config/billion-context/billion-context.json (or the file selected by BILI_CONFIG_FILE), preserving your other settings:

{
  "pi": {
    "subagents": false
  }
}

Restart pi and start a new session for the change to take effect. This disables the three delegate tools, their system-prompt section, and the fleet keyboard shortcut; context compression remains enabled. It does not disable independently installed subagent plugins. More options: subagent configuration.

How sessions work

The proxy keys compression state on the conversation value the client itself provides, verbatim (src/session-id.ts) — no hashing, no protocol/upstream/API-key dimensions (those mutate mid-conversation and orphaned state exactly when users kept talking, #280/#286). The id stays inside the proxy (state store, persistence, UI label); it is never sent upstream.

Where the value comes from, first hit wins: the plugin's x-bili-plugin-conversation (honored only alongside the x-bili-plugin marker header), then per-client headers (x-claude-code-session-id, x-grok-session-id/x-grok-conv-id, x-mavis-session-id, x-opencode-session-id), then generic headers (x-session-affinity, x-acp-session, x-session-id, x-opencode-session, session-id/session_id), then body fields: session_id / metadata.session_id on the Responses wire, and prompt_cache_key promoted over the content-fingerprint fallback on the Responses/OpenAI/Anthropic wires.

Client Sends conversation id? Source
Codex ✅ yes body.session_id / turn-metadata thread id
OpenCode ✅ yes x-opencode-session-id header (ses_…, the request's own session id; 2.x sends the parent's cache-routing affinity in x-session-affinity/X-Session-Id/x-opencode-session alongside it, #2779 — 1.x sent its own id in those instead)
Claude Code ✅ yes x-claude-code-session-id header
omp (via plugin) ✅ yes prompt_cache_key promoted over any fingerprint (#268)
pi (bare) ❌ no nothing → anonymous prefix affinity below

omp caveat (#2583/#3556): on recent OMP builds, default Anthropic (anthropic-messages) requests leave the host through OMP's Cowork transport over node:https directly — they never reach bili's fetch layer, so the prompt_cache_key stamp is withheld there (stamping would leak the field into Anthropic's strict schema → HTTP 400). Since #3556 the bili omp launcher lane no longer leaves that hole open by default: unless you set PI_PROXY / PI_PROXY_ANTHROPIC yourself, the launcher exports PI_PROXY_ANTHROPIC=<proxy>, which pushes Cowork onto Bun's fetch and routes it through the proxy like every other lane (compressed and session-visible; the stamped key is consumed and stripped by the proxy). Direct-and-anonymous remains only for native omp mode and for launcher lanes where you pin your own proxy posture; all other omp traffic keeps its stamped identity. Details: docs/technical-notes.md.

omp advisor isolation (#5567): omp's persistent background streams (e.g. a turn-reviewer advisor on a second model) are separate model conversations, but their Chat Completions requests carry no conversation signal of their own — the plugin stamps the main session's id into prompt_cache_key, so both streams land in ONE bili session. Two models/protocols interleaving into one ledger corrupts it: refs go DEAD (cannot be anchored / content-changed), fold coverage drifts, and usage/window/nudge metering cross-talks between the streams (the log line foreign payload under a shared session id (#4805) marks where the proxy noticed). Until the host-side identity fix lands (tracked in #5567), isolate the advisor by letting it carry its own identity on the wire: in omp's model-registry config (the providers: section of models.yml), set compat.supportsPromptCacheKey: true on the advisor's provider entry — pi-ai then serializes the advisor's own session UUID as prompt_cache_key, and bili binds it to its own session. Boundaries: this does not help if omp explicitly passes a shared cache key for the advisor; once isolated, the advisor runs as its own session with its own compression state; verify via the web panel that advisor traffic appears under a separate session id.

Header-less clients (pi-like): anonymous prefix affinity. With no conversation signal at all, the proxy resolves the session from the replayed history itself (src/prefix-affinity.ts, #309): a request reattaches to a stored session only when its history reproduces that session's message chain byte-exactly from position 0; otherwise it gets its own deterministic pfa-… session. Consequences (#1262): a resumed conversation reattaches to its own session (even after a proxy restart, #499); a new task with an identical opener does NOT inherit another conversation's blocks — it mints a fresh, fully separate session; a request with no usable signal at all gets an explicit 400 instead of silently colliding.

Design record and threat model: docs/session-identity.md. The message-granularity sibling (why identity is content-derived, not an assigned id) is docs/message-identity.md.

For upstream sticky-routing, the proxy forwards only identity values the client already supplied (e.g. a body session_id is forwarded upstream as x-session-id); it never synthesizes one itself.

Recommendation: explicit-id clients are safe to run concurrently. For header-less multi-agent use, prefer the client plugin (stamps a stable id per conversation) or pass an explicit x-acp-session header — otherwise prefix affinity still keeps distinct tasks apart (a diverged fork costs one raw resend plus a compression-ladder restart).

Derived (child) sessions inherit the parent's compressed context (#1333, #1362)

A child session (subagent/fork starting from an empty history) reports its lineage at birth — its identity registration carries parentConversationId and the proxy records a read-only derivedFrom link — so decompress / search_context fall back along the parent chain for content the child never saw itself (cycle-guarded, depth cap 8). Nothing is copied into the child, the parent is never modified; if the parent is unknown the child simply starts fresh. Per-lane parent signals (pi/omp parentSession header, OpenCode V1/V2 parentID): docs/session-identity.md. claude/codex/dsh need nothing here: they share one session id across subagents or have no child-session concept at all.

Running multiple instances (#3633)

One conversation belongs to one instance for its whole life. Fold state, prefix affinity and the summary budget are keyed to a session id whose home is the client's own history — and the session's rows live in that instance's index.db. There is no shared store between instances: nothing replicates, nothing fails over, nothing rehydrates a session onto a different instance.

Consequences for anyone tempted to put several instances behind one Service:

  • Sticky routing is required, and ClientIP affinity is the wrong kind. The conversation identity lives in a header or the request body, not the source IP — a Service can only hash on IP, so a client pinned to replica N silently loses every session when replica N dies (buying throughput while selling away availability, exactly when you scaled out because of load). Correct routing is an L7 proxy hashing a conversation header (x-bili-plugin-conversation, x-opencode-session-id, x-acp-session, …) onto a backend — and the client actually sending one (header-less clients get prefix affinity instead, which an L7 proxy cannot hash).
  • Instance count is volume count. The state directory is one local directory with SQLite in WAL mode (busy_timeout=5000); a coherent shared -shm and working byte-range locks across writers require an RWO volume that is never shared. Pointing two instances at the same RWX/NFS path does not give you a shared store — it gives you silent corruption behind a timeout. One RWO volume per instance, storage.unified included: "unified" means one store for that instance (sessions + CCR + CAS in one index.db), not one store for the fleet.
  • The workload that actually scales is many independent short-lived conversations — one proxy per client or per lane — not one long conversation load-balanced across proxies. Long conversations are single-instance by design.

Single machine, multiple installs (#5046). The topology above covers deployment replicas; one desktop has a sibling situation: two installs on ONE machine (e.g. two DSH profiles — desktop + bot, or a global npm copy beside a host-tree copy) each start their own proxy and, unless isolated, both resolve the SAME default XDG sessions directory and the same config file. Multiple processes writing ONE local-disk index.db is the SUPPORTED topology (#5082/#5091) — SQLite WAL is multi-process safe on a local filesystem — so startup NEVER blocks on a live foreign writer: the peer shows up as an info-level [storage] process pid … is also using … line plus the status wire, nothing more (policy settled 2026-10-31, withdrawing the #5046/B-era refuse-to-start for exactly this shape). What genuinely remains hazardous is two installs walking the SAME session concurrently — that case alarms separately (split-brain contest, #3923). If you still want strictly separate histories and stores per install, give each its own BILI_SESSIONS_DIR (plus BILI_CONFIG_FILE when the config should differ too) through that install's launcher/profile environment — no global env changes needed. Once isolated, the [instances] notice drops off entirely. Note the distinction from the deployment case above: local disk with SQLite WAL tolerates many writers; shared RWX/NFS storage does NOT and keeps requiring one writer per volume.

Naming note: POST /__bili/replicas creates a session checkpoint fork (from stored checkpoints), not a pod replica — read it as /__bili/checkpoints.

The proxy rewrites each session's state file every turn of a long session; on Windows, real-time AV (Defender), the search indexer, or a sync tool (OneDrive) can lock the sessions dir mid-write, so persists fail with EPERM until the lock clears. Fix at the root: add %USERPROFILE%\.local\share\billion-context\ to your antivirus exclusions (Defender steps included) and keep sync tools off that path — docs/configuration.md. The same exclusion also covers the unified-storage index.db refusing to open (unable to open database file, #3823) — the storage-degrade warning names it as the first suspect.

Session file cleanup (#1082)

Short-lived sessions leave small state files behind that are never resumed. Cleanup is opt-in (BILI_SESSION_GC=1; off by default — session files are user data, no silent deletion policy): when enabled, bili sweeps the sessions dir at boot and hourly and deletes a file only when BOTH hold — older than BILI_SESSION_GC_MAX_AGE_DAYS (default 7 days) AND never compressed with its newest request body ≤ BILI_SESSION_GC_MAX_TOKENS tokens (default 1M) — so deletion loses nothing but bytes. CCR content stores follow their session file's lifecycle; compressed sessions are never deleted; every deletion is audit-logged. Full policy: docs/configuration.md.

Storage maintenance CLI (#3928)

The same store maintenance the panel exposes over HTTP (POST /__bili/storage/gc, POST /__bili/storage/restore) has a thin CLI layer — no proxy needed, run it on any machine that owns the sessions dir:

bili sessions ls                 # id, label, decoded size, last-updated, storage status (active/archived)
bili sessions rm <id>            # full delete (content refcount release incl. media); shrinks index.db afterwards (--no-vacuum skips)
bili sessions archive <id>       # export to archive/archive.jsonl + sweep rows; tombstone keeps label & identity
bili sessions restore <id>       # bring an archived session back from the log line
bili sessions foreign-blocks     # (#5312) list fold blocks whose covered messages never belonged to this transcript — dry-run; --apply reversibly archives them, --restore <sid>:<bid> brings one back
bili storage gc [--days N] [--vacuum full|incremental] [--dry-run]
                                 # print the sweep plan (sessions past retention, zero-ref content rows, ~pages reclaimable), then run the same gc() the HTTP endpoint calls; --dry-run stops after the plan
bili storage backup [--keep N]   # online-consistent index.db snapshot into <sessions>/backups/ (VACUUM INTO —
                                 # never rewrites the source, no exclusive lock, safe while a proxy runs); the
                                 # snapshot is quick_check-verified before it counts; keeps the newest N (default 3)
bili storage repair [--from f.db] # with --from: verify the backup (quick_check + readable sessions), quarantine the
                                 # broken index.db IN PLACE (index.db.corrupt-<ts>, evidence kept), copy the backup in
                                 # (the backup itself stays untouched), verify again; without --from: salvage the
                                 # corrupt file row-by-row into a freshly-migrated schema (bisects broken page ranges
                                 # to single rows; a corrupt overflow cell nulls its own column, the rest of the row
                                 # survives). Both swap paths refuse to run while another live process holds index.db.lock.

archive/restore/gc require the unified store (BILI_STORAGE_UNIFIED=sqlite|shadow|full or storage.unified in the config file — the default is now pure sqlite) — legacy-only installs refuse with a hint. --days defaults to storage.archiveAfterDays (365). No scheduler: these run on demand. All commands accept --json.

Backup & repair (#7156, 2026-11-20 production incident). A 3.2 GB index.db proved corrupt (foreign second writer, #7156) and the only recovery path was a hand-rolled .recover-equivalent plus manual file surgery — those two manual moves are now the backup/repair commands above. Operational discipline that keeps the incident from recurring: run bili storage backup on a schedule (the retention flag is the only state it keeps), and keep exactly one long-lived bili process per sessions dir — a second live writer is the corruption mode, and every storage command now detects a live foreign writer and refuses rather than contending.

Full vacuum is an offline operation on large databases (#4612). --vacuum full (the default) rewrites the entire index.db under an exclusive write lock — O(db size), minutes to tens of minutes on multi-GB databases, with no intermediate progress (SQLite's VACUUM is atomic; it cannot be split). Running it while a proxy is serving from the same sessions dir starves that proxy's writes until its storage layer degrades, so storage gc --vacuum full refuses to start when another live process holds the database (index.db.lock pid discipline, #4175): the CLI exits 1 with an actionable message, the panel endpoint returns HTTP 409. Stop the other instance first (or wait for it to exit) and retry; for online-safe shrink use --vacuum incremental, which reclaims freed pages in short transactions without taking the exclusive lock. The zero-ref delete sweep itself is batched with per-batch progress output either way.

Status

Early. Protocol handling and compression work against mock tests (500+ passing). Real-model integration testing is the next milestone. Expect rough edges.

Client-side plugins for pi / omp / opencode ship inside billion-context (dist/agent/*.js) for the cooperative-proxy path. See the "Which do I need?" section above for how billion-context, the standalone billion-context-pi, and opencode-acp relate.

Attribution requirement (one term on top of MIT)

This project is MIT-licensed plus one additional term: any product or service (commercial or open source) whose users can see or interact with it and which uses this software must attribute it — stating that it uses billion-context with a link back to this repository — on its home page, documentation, or About/Credits page. Pure server-side/embedded use satisfies this via shipped documentation. See the Additional Term at the end of LICENSE.

If you build on this project, we'd love to hear about it: open an issue (no obligation) so we can track where it's used.

License

MIT

item.title: lobehub/lobehub
item.description:
🤯 LobeHub - Super-Agents on Your Team. Add super-agents to the chats your team already uses.They take on work by themselves and get better every week.

https://lobehub.com

LobeHub

Super-Agents on Your Team

Add super-agents to the chats your team already uses.
They take on work by themselves and get better every week.

English · 简体中文 · Official Site · Changelog · Documents · Blog · Feedback




Share LobeHub Repository

Table of contents

TOC

  • 👋🏻 Getting Started & Join Our Community
  • ✨ Features
    • From new hire to one of the team
    • Day 1 Welcome to the team
    • Week 1 Its first task
    • Month 1–2 Settling in as the team grows
    • Month 3 It passes its review
    • Bring them onto your team
  • 🧩 Marketplace
  • 📖 Documentation
  • 🛳 Self Hosting
    • A Docker Compose (recommended)
    • B One-click deploy
  • ⌨️ Local Development
  • 🤝 Contributing
  • ❤️ Sponsor
  • 🔬 Research



https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0a33365f-b786-48b5-9ed6-f8af7927bccb

👋🏻 Getting Started & Join Our Community

We are a group of e/acc design-engineers, hoping to provide modern design components and tools for AIGC.

Whether for users or professional developers, LobeHub will be your AI Agent playground. Please be aware that LobeHub is currently under active development, and feedback is welcome for any issues encountered.

We are live on Product Hunt! We are thrilled to bring LobeHub to the world. If you believe in a future where humans and agents co-evolve, please support our journey.
Join our Discord community! This is where you can connect with developers and other enthusiastic users of LobeHub.

Important

Star Us, You will receive all release notifications from GitHub without any delay ~ ⭐️

Star History

✨ Features

From new hire to one of the team

See what Lobe AI gets done, from its first day in your team chat onward.

WHAT MAKES A SUPER-AGENT

🔌 Flexible access
Plug in any IM app, agent or model, all in one place. 		⚡ Parallel work
Runs several tasks at once, so you don't have to chase each one.
🙋 Finds its own work
Takes on the tasks that suit it, without someone passing messages along. 		📈 Gets more expert
The more you use it, the faster an agent builds up its expertise.

Day 1 Welcome to the team

You add it to your team chat and ask it to read up. By lunch it has gone through the history and said hello to everyone.

Week 1 Its first task

Someone posts a feature request in Discord and nobody assigns it. Lobe AI takes it on, and you only step in once, to accept the result.

Month 1–2 Settling in as the team grows

Everyone now has their own agent, and design, releases and docs each have a dedicated one. Lobe AI is still learning when to speak up and when to stay quiet.

Month 3 It passes its review

When it started, it got about half of these right. Now it rarely misses, and every correction you gave it has become a lesson it keeps.

Bring them onto your team

Start with one, and add more when you need them.

Try LobeHub Cloud · Self-host it

Contact: business@lobehub.com

🧩 Marketplace

Find agents, MCP servers and skills on lobehub.com, add them to your workspace, or publish your own.

Market What you'll find
🤖 Agents Ready-to-use agents for writing, Q&A, images, video, voice and workflows. Add one to your workspace and adapt it.
🔌 MCP Servers MCP servers rated on activity, stability and community feedback, so you can pick ones you can trust.
🧠 Skills Agent skills in the open SKILL.md format. They also work in Claude Code, Codex CLI and ChatGPT.
🎨 AI / LLM Icons A free icon set for major AI brands and models, with SVG, PNG and vector downloads.

Publish your own

  • Agents: submit one from its settings in LobeHub. The Creator Reward Program features a community agent every two weeks.

  • MCP servers: ask your agent to Read https://lobehub.com/publish-mcp/skill.md and follow the instructions to publish my MCP server to the LobeHub Marketplace, or use the CLI:

    npx -y @lobehub/market-cli login
npx -y @lobehub/market-cli plugin submit https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY

  • Skills: submit a GitHub repository from the Skills marketplace.

📖 Documentation

All documentation lives at lobehub.com/docs:

Section What's covered
Get LobeHub Web, macOS, Windows, Linux and mobile apps, and where work runs
Lobe AI The built-in agent: chat, code, research and write with no setup
Agents System role, model, skills, connectors, web search, resources and memory
Agent Team Several agents working together: sequential, parallel, iterative or debate
Connect External Agents Bring in Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes and more, with project context and permissions
Tasks Delegate work, track status, follow up in comments, run once or on a schedule
Memory Structured memories you can review, edit and delete
Pages Write long documents with agents, in Markdown
Resource Library Documents, generated images and drafts your agents can answer from
Channels Your own bots on Discord, Slack, Telegram, LINE, QQ, WeChat, Feishu and Lark
Messenger Chat with your agents through LobeHub's bot on Telegram, Slack, Discord and WeChat
GitHub Integration Track agents' pull requests; merging accepts the work, failed checks go back to the agent
Marketplace Community agents, MCP servers and skills
Model Providers Setup guides for 40+ providers, inference platforms and local models
Self-Hosting Docker Compose, Vercel and other deployment platforms
Environment Variables Every configuration option, including model providers
Authentication Sign-in with Better Auth and SSO providers such as Auth0
Development Tech stack, local setup and contribution guidelines

🛳 Self Hosting

Run LobeHub on your own infrastructure and keep your data with you. The full guide is in 📘 Build your own LobeHub.

A Docker Compose (recommended)

Starts LobeHub with PostgreSQL, Redis, RustFS file storage, SearXNG search and the agent gateway. Runs on Linux and macOS, or on Windows through WSL 2.

mkdir lobehub && cd lobehub
bash <(curl -fsSL https://lobe.li/setup.sh) -l en
docker compose up -d

Then open http://localhost:3210. Ports, LAN and domain modes, and upgrades are covered in the 📘 Docker Compose guide.

B One-click deploy

Vercel needs a PostgreSQL database, S3-compatible storage and a few secrets before you deploy. The 📘 Vercel guide walks through each one.

Deploy with Vercel Deploy with Zeabur Deploy with Sealos Deploy with RepoCloud Deploy with Alibaba Cloud

⌨️ Local Development

You can use GitHub Codespaces for online development:

Or clone it for local development:

$ git clone https://github.com/lobehub/lobehub.git
$ cd lobehub
$ pnpm install
$ bun run dev       # Full-stack (Next.js + Vite SPA)
$ bun run dev:spa   # SPA frontend only (port 9876)

Debug Proxy: After running dev:spa, the terminal prints a proxy URL like https://app.lobehub.com/_dangerous_local_dev_proxy?debug-host=http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A9876. Open it to develop locally against the production backend with HMR — a development convenience, not a place to verify a change.

If you would like to learn more details, please feel free to look at our 📘 Development Guide.

🤝 Contributing

Contributions of all types are more than welcome; if you are interested in contributing code, feel free to check out our GitHub Issues and Projects to get stuck in to show us what you're made of.

Tip

We are creating a technology-driven forum, fostering knowledge interaction and the exchange of ideas that may culminate in mutual inspiration and collaborative innovation.

Help us make LobeHub better. Welcome to provide product design feedback, user experience discussions directly to us.

Principal Maintainers: @arvinxx @canisminor1990

❤️ Sponsor

Every bit counts and your one-time donation sparkles in our galaxy of support! You're a shooting star, making a swift and bright impact on our journey. Thank you for believing in us – your generosity guides us toward our mission, one brilliant flash at a time.

🔬 Research

  • 📊 MCPMark: A stress-testing benchmark for MCP. Its tasks are realistic, multi-step and verifiable, covering file systems, databases, Playwright browser automation, GitHub and more. Built by EVAL SYS, LobeHub and the National University of Singapore, and open source under Apache-2.0.
  • 📄 Research paper: Read our research paper on Hugging Face Papers.
  • 🧪 EVAL SYS: An evaluation systems organization, one of the teams behind MCPMark.

📝 License

Copyright © 2026 LobeHub.
This project is LobeHub Community License licensed.

item.title: ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui
item.description:
AG-UI: the Agent-User Interaction Protocol. Bring Agents into Frontend Applications.

https://ag-ui.com

The open protocol that connects any agent to any app.

Docs · Examples · Spec · Discord


AG-UI is an open, lightweight, event-based protocol that standardizes how AI agents connect to user-facing applications.

Agents don't fit the request/response model. They stream tokens, call tools mid-response, update shared state, pause for a human, and spawn subagents, and every framework does it differently. AG-UI replaces that custom wiring with one bi-directional event stream: the agent emits typed events, and any client can render them, no matter which framework built the agent. The same agent can power a web app, a mobile app, a terminal, or Slack.

Important

AG-UI 1.0 is here. The protocol now has a stable, frozen specification backed by a JSON Schema, and the TypeScript, Python, and .NET SDKs are generated from it. 1.0 is backwards compatible in both directions: 0.x agents work with 1.0 clients and vice versa. What changed → · Migration guide →

Quick start

Start a new app. The CLI scaffolds a frontend (CopilotKit on Next.js, or a terminal client) wired to the agent framework you pick:

npx create-ag-ui-app@latest

Then follow the printed next steps. The generated templates call OpenAI, so set your key before npm run dev:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
Or speak the protocol directly: a 30-line agent server and client

An AG-UI agent is any HTTP endpoint that accepts a RunAgentInput and streams events back. No API keys needed for this one.

1. The agent (Python). Requires Python 3.9+.

pip install ag-ui-protocol fastapi uvicorn

# server.py
import uuid

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from ag_ui.core import (
    PROTOCOL_VERSION,
    RunAgentInput,
    RunStartedEvent,
    RunFinishedEvent,
    TextMessageStartEvent,
    TextMessageContentEvent,
    TextMessageEndEvent,
)
from ag_ui.encoder import EventEncoder

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/")
async def run_agent(input_data: RunAgentInput, request: Request):
    encoder = EventEncoder(accept=request.headers.get("accept"))

    async def events():
        yield encoder.encode(RunStartedEvent(
            thread_id=input_data.thread_id,
            run_id=input_data.run_id,
            protocol_version=PROTOCOL_VERSION,
        ))
        message_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
        yield encoder.encode(TextMessageStartEvent(message_id=message_id, role="assistant"))
        for chunk in ["Hello ", "from ", "AG-UI!"]:
            yield encoder.encode(TextMessageContentEvent(message_id=message_id, delta=chunk))
        yield encoder.encode(TextMessageEndEvent(message_id=message_id))
        yield encoder.encode(RunFinishedEvent(thread_id=input_data.thread_id, run_id=input_data.run_id))

    return StreamingResponse(events(), media_type=encoder.get_content_type())

uvicorn server:app --port 8000

2. The client (TypeScript). In a second terminal, in a new folder. Requires Node.js 20+.

npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module
npm install @ag-ui/client tsx

// client.ts
import { HttpAgent } from "@ag-ui/client";

const agent = new HttpAgent({ url: "http://localhost:8000/" });

agent.addMessage({ id: crypto.randomUUID(), role: "user", content: "Hi there!" });

await agent.runAgent({}, {
  onRunStartedEvent: ({ event }) => console.log(`run started (AG-UI ${event.protocolVersion})`),
  onTextMessageContentEvent: ({ event }) => { process.stdout.write(event.delta); },
  onRunFinishedEvent: () => console.log("\nrun finished"),
});

npx tsx client.ts

You should see Hello from AG-UI! stream in. Swap the server for any supported framework and the client doesn't change.

Where AG-UI fits

AG-UI is one of three open, complementary agentic protocols. MCP gives agents tools and context, A2A lets agents work with other agents, and AG-UI brings agents to users. A single agent often uses all three, and AG-UI can front agents that speak MCP or A2A. Read more →

Note

AG-UI or A2UI? They work together. A2UI, MCP Apps, and Open-JSON-UI are generative UI specs: they describe what UI an agent wants to show. AG-UI is the runtime protocol that carries those payloads, along with everything else, between the agent and the app. Learn more →

Integrations

AG-UI is adopted by Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle, and built into most agent frameworks. Every framework below has a live demo in the Dojo.


LangChain
Docs · Demo
CrewAI
Docs · Demo
Microsoft Agent Framework
Docs · Demo
Google ADK
Docs · Demo

AWS Strands Agents
Docs · Demo
Mastra
Docs · Demo
Pydantic AI
Docs · Demo
LlamaIndex
Docs · Demo

Agno
Docs · Demo
AG2
Docs · Demo
Claude Agent SDK
Docs · Demo
+11 more
Antigravity, OpenAI Agents, watsonx, Spring AI, and others in the full list

Protocols: A2A · MCP · MCP Apps · A2UI
Clients: CopilotKit (React, Angular, Vue, React Native) · Slack & Teams · Terminal · OpenBot

Don't see your framework? Build an integration →

Full list of integrations

Show all integrations
  • Partners: LangChain · CrewAI
  • Built in: Microsoft Agent Framework · Google ADK (JS) · Google Antigravity · AWS Strands Agents · Mastra · Pydantic AI · Agno · LlamaIndex · AG2
  • More frameworks: Claude Agent SDK · Claude Managed Agents · IBM watsonx Orchestrate · Langroid · Spring AI · Cloudflare Agents · Omnara · Genkit (Go) · OpenAI Agents
  • Specs: Oracle Agent Spec
  • Deployment: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Source for every integration lives in integrations/ and middlewares/, and the demos in apps/dojo.

SDKs

Language Install Reference
TypeScript npm install @ag-ui/client Docs · Source
Python pip install ag-ui-protocol Docs · Source
.NET dotnet add package AGUI.Client Docs · Source

Community SDKs: Kotlin · Go · Java · Dart · Rust · Ruby · C++ · Swift

Features: what you can build

Each building block maps to events in the spec, and each has a live demo in the AG-UI Dojo.

Building block What it does Try it
Streaming chat Token-by-token messages across multi-turn sessions, with cancel and resume Demo
Generative UI Agents render typed components, or declarative UI with A2UI and MCP Apps Demo
Shared state A typed store the agent and app both read and write, synced with snapshots and JSON Patch deltas Demo
Frontend tools The agent calls tools that run in the app, and gets the result back Demo
Human in the loop Runs end with an interrupt outcome; the user approves, edits, or rejects, and the next run resumes Demo
Reasoning Show the agent's reasoning as it works, including encrypted reasoning round-trips Demo
Subagents Nested delegation, with every event attributed to the subagent run that produced it Demo
Multimodal Images, audio, video, and documents in user input and tool results Demo

Tool output streaming, backend tool rendering, activity progress, token usage, and custom events are covered in the docs. Here's a quick tour of the Dojo:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c298eea8-3f39-4a94-b968-7712429b0c49

How it works

Your app starts a run by sending the agent a single RunAgentInput: the conversation, the tools the frontend offers, shared state, and context. The agent answers with a stream of typed events from eight families: run lifecycle, text messages, tool calls, state, reasoning, activity, subagents, and custom events (full list). Only the run lifecycle is required, so a minimal agent emits a handful of events and grows from there.

AG-UI is transport-agnostic. The spec defines HTTP + SSE and a binary HTTP + Protobuf binding, and middleware can adapt events from any source. Read the architecture overview for the full picture.

Event reference

AG-UI 1.0 defines 31 event types in eight families. See the spec for every field.

Event family Events
Runs and steps RUN_STARTED RUN_FINISHED RUN_ERROR STEP_STARTED STEP_FINISHED
Text messages TEXT_MESSAGE_START TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT TEXT_MESSAGE_END TEXT_MESSAGE_CHUNK
Tool calls TOOL_CALL_START TOOL_CALL_ARGS TOOL_CALL_END TOOL_CALL_RESULT TOOL_CALL_CHUNK
State STATE_SNAPSHOT STATE_DELTA (JSON Patch) MESSAGES_SNAPSHOT
Reasoning REASONING_START REASONING_MESSAGE_* REASONING_ENCRYPTED_VALUE REASONING_END
Activity ACTIVITY_SNAPSHOT ACTIVITY_DELTA
Subagents SUBAGENT_STARTED SUBAGENT_FINISHED SUBAGENT_ERROR
Passthrough RAW CUSTOM

Community

  • Questions and ideas: Discord and GitHub Discussions
  • Bugs: GitHub Issues
  • What's next: the roadmap and the draft spec

Contributing

Contributions are welcome: new integrations, SDKs, docs, and fixes. Start with CONTRIBUTING.md, and use the server starter and middleware starter as templates for new integrations. Report security issues as described in SECURITY.md.

AG-UI was created by CopilotKit and is developed in the open with the community.

License

AG-UI is open source under the MIT License.

The open-source repo for docs.github.com

https://docs.github.com

GitHub Docs

Welcome to GitHub Docs! GitHub’s documentation is open source, meaning anyone from inside or outside the company can contribute. For full contributing guidelines, visit our contributing guide.

Quick links by contributor type

  • Hubbers (GitHub employees): See CONTRIBUTING.md in the docs-content repository for GitHub-specific processes.

  • Open source contributors: See CONTRIBUTING.md in the docs repository for a quick-start summary.

How we sync changes across Docs repositories

There are two GitHub Docs repositories:

  • github/docs (public): Open to external contributions

  • github/docs-internal (private): For GitHub employee contributions.

The two repositories sync frequently. Content changes in one are reflected in the other. Hubbers might prefer to post in docs when working with a customer, but docs has limitations on the types of contributions it accepts to safeguard the site and our workflows. Internal contributions should usually go to docs-internal.

Important: The docs repository accepts contributions to content files (.md files in /content and select /data sections like reusables only). Infrastructure files, workflows, and site-building code are not open for external modification.

New to contributing

Here are some resources to help you get started with open source contributions:

  • Finding ways to contribute to open source on GitHub

item.title: anthropics/sandbox-runtime
item.description:
A lightweight sandboxing tool for enforcing filesystem and network restrictions on arbitrary processes at the OS level, without requiring a container.

Anthropic Sandbox Runtime (srt)

A lightweight sandboxing tool for enforcing filesystem and network restrictions on arbitrary processes at the OS level, without requiring a container.

srt uses native OS sandboxing primitives (sandbox-exec on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux) and proxy-based network filtering. It can be used to sandbox the behaviour of agents, local MCP servers, bash commands and arbitrary processes.

Beta Research Preview

The Sandbox Runtime is a research preview developed for Claude Code to enable safer AI agents. It's being made available as an early open source preview to help the broader ecosystem build more secure agentic systems. As this is an early research preview, APIs and configuration formats may evolve. We welcome feedback and contributions to make AI agents safer by default!

Installation

npm install -g @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime

Basic Usage

# Network restrictions
$ srt "curl anthropic.com"
Running: curl anthropic.com
<html>...</html>  # Request succeeds

$ srt "curl example.com"
Running: curl example.com
Connection blocked by network allowlist  # Request blocked

# Filesystem restrictions
$ srt "cat README.md"
Running: cat README.md
# Anthropic Sandb...  # Current directory access allowed

$ srt "cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa"
Running: cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa
cat: /Users/ollie/.ssh/id_rsa: Operation not permitted  # Specific file blocked

Overview

This package provides a standalone sandbox implementation that can be used as both a CLI tool and a library. It's designed with a secure-by-default philosophy tailored for common developer use cases: processes start with minimal access, and you explicitly poke only the holes you need.

Key capabilities:

  • Network restrictions: Control which hosts/domains can be accessed via HTTP/HTTPS and other protocols
  • Filesystem restrictions: Control which files/directories can be read/written
  • Unix socket restrictions: Control access to local IPC sockets
  • Violation monitoring: On macOS, tap into the system's sandbox violation log store for real-time alerts

Example Use Case: Sandboxing MCP Servers

A key use case is sandboxing Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to restrict their capabilities. For example, to sandbox the filesystem MCP server:

Without sandboxing (.mcp.json):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem"]
    }
  }
}

With sandboxing (.mcp.json):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": {
      "command": "srt",
      "args": ["npx", "-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem"]
    }
  }
}

Then configure restrictions in ~/.srt-settings.json:

{
  "filesystem": {
    "denyRead": [],
    "allowWrite": ["."],
    "denyWrite": ["~/sensitive-folder"]
  },
  "network": {
    "allowedDomains": [],
    "deniedDomains": []
  }
}

Now the MCP server will be blocked from writing to the denied path:

> Write a file to ~/sensitive-folder
✗ Error: EPERM: operation not permitted, open '/Users/ollie/sensitive-folder/test.txt'

How It Works

The sandbox uses OS-level primitives to enforce restrictions that apply to the entire process tree:

  • macOS: Uses sandbox-exec with dynamically generated Seatbelt profiles
  • Linux: Uses bubblewrap for containerization with network namespace isolation
